cards.title: A Human-Centered Framework for Exploring and Steering LLM Internals: A Case Study of Bias in Essay Scoring

rows.value: S2W-4A5F4A3A261E38008BFFAD02
other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper is conceptually grounded in human-centered AI transparency, explainable-AI sensemaking and mental-model formation, Value Sensitive Design, and sociotechnical fairness. It uses those traditions to frame a five-stage interpretability workflow in which probing, attribution patching, and steering support human inquiry and normative judgment. These traditions are conceptually used rather than operationalized as measured theoretical constructs: the case tests model-level representational and intervention effects, but it does not test end-user workflow, learning, capability growth, or transfer.

medium · The model-level measurements are directly reported, but they come from one corpus, one Llama model family, one demographic dimension, and researcher-operated interventions. The five-stage workflow and its interface implications have not been validated with end-user practitioners, and no learning or transfer outcomes were measured.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-C01-FRAMEWORK
items.small: concept or lineage, principle, mechanism, condition, open question
items.lead: This is a transferable workflow scaffold for human inquiry: established technical methods become supports for progressive sensemaking, hypothesis testing, control assessment, and value-laden judgment. It proposes a redistribution of cognitive work between practitioner and tool, but the paper demonstrates the sequence only through researcher-led analysis and does not establish end-user workflow, learning, or capability effects.

rows.value: The authors frame interpretability as a five-stage process of noticing value tensions, building mental models, interrogating causality, exploring controllability, and making normative judgments, and argue that tools should support iterative movement among observation, experimentation, and reflection rather than static inspection.

(PDF p. 1) Abstract, opening paragraph — The authors define interpretability as a five-stage sensemaking, experimentation, and judgment process.
quotes: We present a human-centered framework that reframes interpretability as a process of sensemaking, experimentation, and judgment through five stages: noticing value tensions, building mental models, interrogating causality, exploring controllability, and making normative judgments.

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Section 3, opening paragraph — The authors frame engagement with LLM internals as human sensemaking and claim applicability beyond the demonstrated bias case.
quotes: We conceptualize engagement with LLM internals not as a technical pipeline, but as a process of human sensemaking and judgment. We articulate a five-stage framework capturing how practitioners come to notice, interrogate, and shape model behavior (Figure 1). While we illustrate each stage through our bias case study, the framework generalizes to any scenario in which practitioners seek to understand and address undesirable model behavior.

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Section 3, Stage 2: Building Mental Models — The authors position linear probing as cognitive scaffolding for tentative mental-model formation and sensemaking.
quotes: Stage 2: Building Mental Models. Practitioners construct tentative mental models of the system’s internal reasoning. Techniques like linear probing [1] scaffold this cognitive process, supporting questions such as: Is specific information explicitly represented? Which layers are most sensitive? Probing supports sensemaking rather than merely producing measurements [18].

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Section 5, Support Exploratory Practice, Not Static Inspection — The authors propose tool support for fluid movement between observation, experimentation, and reflection as practitioner needs evolve.
quotes: Current tools emphasize visualization and inspection (heatmaps, attribution plots). Our case study shows practitioners’ needs evolve—from noticing behavior, to hypothesis formation, to causal testing, to evaluating trade-offs. Tools should support iterative exploration, enabling fluid movement between observation, experimentation, and reflection [12].

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Section 6, second limitation — The interventions were researcher-led and the framework has not been validated through a realized interface with end-user practitioners.
quotes: Second, interventions were performed by technically skilled researchers rather than through a realized user-facing interface; the framework has not yet been validated with end-user practitioners. We plan to conduct a formative study with 10–15 ML practitioners using think-aloud protocols and semi-structured interviews to examine how they navigate the five stages, where they encounter difficulties, and what tool support would be most valuable.

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Section 6, first limitation — The case is limited to essay scoring, Llama 3.1, and ELL status, with broader generalizability unresolved.
quotes: First, our case study focuses on a single domain (essay scoring), a single model family (Llama 3.1), and a single demographic dimension (ELL status). The framework’s generalizability to other domains, such as healthcare or hiring, other model architectures, such as GPT or Claude, and other types of undesirable behavior, such as hallucination or safety violations, requires further investigation.

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Section 2, Human-centered AI transparency paragraph — The authors ground the work in human-centered AI transparency, where interpretability is experiential and shaped by interaction, citing references 6 and 12.

Work on explainable AI has shown that effective tools should support sensemaking and mental model formation [11, 18]. We extend this tradition by examining how practitioners engage with LLM internals during system development—framing interpretability not as static inspection, but as an exploratory relationship involving experimentation and value-laden decision-making.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-C03-CONTROLLABILITY
items.lead: This yields a design-space principle: intervention controls should be represented as directional and dependent on model training state, because having a control does not imply symmetric efficacy. The artifact-level asymmetry is measured, but the paper does not show that visualizing it improves practitioner expectations or decisions.

rows.value: Layer-25 activation steering was directionally asymmetric: positive steering produced much larger score shifts than negative steering, with a 4:1 ratio that fell to 1.3:1 after fine-tuning. items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-C04-STEERING-BENEFIT
items.lead: In this bounded condition, an internal intervention improved both a fairness-related artifact measure and task-performance alignment rather than forcing a trade-off. The evidence is an immediate model-output result under active steering, not evidence of durable deployment reliability, practitioner learning, or general transfer.

(PDF p. 3) Section 4.5, Making Normative Judgments, opening paragraph — Negative Layer-25 steering without demographic prompts reduced score gaps and increased correlation with human scores in both model variants.
quotes: Applying negative steering (𝛼=1.5) at Layer 25 to ELL essays scored without demographic prompts reduced the ELL–Non-ELL score gap by 83.3% (base model) and 70.8% (fine-tuned). Crucially, this intervention did not come at the cost of performance; instead, it improved scoring accuracy. The correlation with human scores increased from 0.350 to 0.423 (+0.073) in the base model and from 0.393 to 0.443 (+0.050) in the fine-tuned model.

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Section 4.5, dual-mechanism result — The beneficial no-demographic-prompt result does not extend to explicit ELL prompting, where compensation was not reduced.

When steering was applied to essays scored with explicit ELL information in the prompt, the compensation effect was not reduced but slightly increased, yielding a negative cancellation rate (–31.8% in the base model). Determining appropriate intervention thus required interpretive judgment about trade-offs, not mere optimization.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-C05-DUAL-PATHWAY

cards.title: Revisiting the Hint Button: Consistent Negative Associations Between Unproductive Hint Use and Learning Outcomes in Intelligent Tutoring Systems

rows.value: other
primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method, design principle

Three semesters of log data from a K-12 decimals game built on an intelligent tutoring system, 999 students of 1,370, asking what on-demand hints actually do. The system works on average: pretest 22.17 of 52 points, immediate posttest 24.88, one-week delayed posttest 25.30, a large pre-to-post effect. The average hides everything, because the standard deviation of the gain, 6.39 points, is more than twice the mean gain of 2.71. Two behaviours computed from ordinary logs explain part of the spread and both point the same way. Asking for a hint before making any attempt, and clicking past hints faster than the words could be read at four words a second, each correlate negatively with the pretest, the posttest and the one-week delayed posttest in all three cohorts, from -0.567 to -0.766, and each stays a significant negative predictor after prior knowledge is controlled. The students who do it most are the ones with the least prior knowledge, so the authors conclude that freely available hints may widen rather than close the gap. Their explanation is about the interface, not the learner: a persistent hint button is an affordance for bypass, and for a student who clicks straight to the bottom-out hint the tutor is effectively a screen that displays the answer before the problem starts. It is correlational, from observational data, and the authors say so.

medium · The strongest evidence in this corpus for help degrading the learning it was built to support, and it is still correlational. What it has: 999 students across three cohorts and 4 to 6 schools per semester, counterbalanced test versions, a one-week delayed posttest taken away from the system, indicators computed from complete interaction logs, and eighteen coefficients that all point the same way at p < .001. What it does not have: any manipulation of hint availability, so the causal direction is open and the authors state that plainly. The obvious confound is prior knowledge, and controlling for the pretest does not remove the association but does not exclude a third factor such as disengagement either. Two further gaps matter. The abstract says the associations are particularly pronounced among lower-knowledge learners, and no interaction or subgroup model is reported; only the frequency of the behaviour is shown to differ by quartile. And the cohorts are described as the three semesters with hint access, implying no-hint semesters that are never compared. Carry the replicated negative associations and the affordance argument; do not carry a causal effect of hints.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The most direct evidence in this corpus that help can be consumed in a way that predicts worse capability once the help is gone, and it is measured that way: the posttest and the one-week delayed posttest are paper tests taken in class, away from the tutor, so every coefficient describes unsupported performance. Two behaviours read off ordinary logs, asking before attempting and clicking past hints faster than they can be read, correlate negatively with the pretest, the immediate posttest and the delayed posttest in each of three cohorts, from -0.567 to -0.766, and each remains a significant negative predictor once the pretest is controlled. Eighteen coefficients, all negative, all at p < .001, across 999 students and up to six schools a semester. What it is not is a demonstration that hints caused the damage. Nothing was manipulated; a student who leans on hints and a student who learns little may simply be the same student, and one prior-knowledge covariate does not exclude that. The defensible carry is that heavy, shallow help use marks a trajectory towards poor unsupported performance, and that it is cheap to detect.

(PDF p. 1) Abstract, the finding — The headline: across 999 K-12 mathematics students, premature hint requests and superficial hint reading are consistently associated with reduced learning gains across cohorts, persisting after prior knowledge is controlled and said to be pronounced among lower-knowledge learners.
quotes: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) commonly provide on-demand multi-level hints designed to scaffold learning, yet their relation- ship with learning outcomes remains complex. While unproductive hint-use behaviors are well documented, existing detection meth- ods often rely on sophisticated models or tutor-specific features that hinder broader adoption. Through a multi-semester analysis of 999 K–12 mathematics students, this study demonstrates that sim- ple, interpretable indicators of unproductive hint use—premature hint requests and superficial hint reading—are consistently associ- ated with reduced learning gains across cohorts. These associations persist after controlling for prior knowledge and are particularly pronounced among learners with lower prior knowledge

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) Results, the regressions for premature hint requests — Two OLS models on the Spring 2021 cohort: premature hint use stays a significant negative predictor of the posttest and, more strongly, of the one-week delayed posttest after the pretest is controlled, with the models explaining about two-thirds of the variance.
quotes: To complement our non-parametric correlational analysis and to estimate the relationship between unproductive hint usage and subsequent performance while controlling for prior knowledge, we conducted two ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analyses. Despite violations of univariate normality in the key variables, OLS regression is generally robust in large samples (𝑁= 277), allowing estimation of associations while controlling for covariates. The first model predicted posttest scores from unproductive hint count, con- trolling for pretest scores. The model was significant and explained a substantial portion of the variance (𝑅2 = 0.667, 𝐹(2, 274) = 274.9, 𝑝< 0.001). First, as expected, pretest scores were a strong pos- itive predictor of posttest scores (𝛽= 0.70, 𝑝< 0.001). Second, even after controlling for prior knowledge, unproductive hint us- age remained a significant negative predictor of posttest scores (𝛽= −0.28, 𝑝< 0.001). A second model predicting delayed posttest scores yielded a similar pattern (𝑅2 = 0.685), with pretest scores again showing a strong positive relationship (𝛽= 0.69, 𝑝< 0.001) and unproductive hint usage showing an even stronger negative coefficient (𝛽= −0.37, 𝑝< 0.001). These results reinforce the find- ings from our correlational analysis, suggesting that unproductive hint-seeking is not merely a correlate of low prior knowledge, but shows independent associations with poorer learning outcomes and retention

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Results, superficial reading against later performance — Quick hint reading correlates negatively with both the immediate and the delayed posttest, and remains a significant negative predictor of both after prior knowledge is controlled.
quotes: Next, we examined the relationship between quick hint reading and subsequent performance. Spearman correlations revealed that this behavior was negatively correlated with posttest scores (𝜌= −0.677, 𝑝< 0.001) and delayed posttest scores (𝜌= −0.644, 𝑝< 0.001), indicating it is strongly associated with poorer learning outcomes and reduced knowledge retention

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Results, the replication across three cohorts — The replication stated cohort by cohort: strong negative correlations with pretest, posttest and delayed posttest for both behaviours across all three semesters, with significant negative regression coefficients surviving the pretest control everywhere.
quotes: For premature hint requests, Spearman correlations with pretest scores ranged from 𝜌= −0.567 to −0.697 (𝑝< 0.001), indicating a consistently strong negative relationship between prior knowledge and this behavior across all three cohorts. Similarly, correlations with posttest (𝜌= −0.616 to −0.704) and delayed posttest scores (𝜌= −0.606 to −0.694) remained strongly negative and statisti- cally significant. More importantly, even after controlling for prior knowledge through OLS regression, premature hint requests con- tinued to significantly negatively predict both posttest (𝛽= −0.14 to −0.28) and delayed posttest scores (𝛽= −0.17 to −0.37). The pattern for superficial hint reading was similarly consistent. Correlations with pretest scores ranged from 𝜌= −0.656 to −0.744 (𝑝< 0.001). The regression coefficients (𝛽= −0.06 to −0.11 for posttest; 𝛽= −0.08 to −0.14 for delayed posttest) remained statis- tically significant across all semesters after controlling for pretest performance

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Discussion, the headline reading — The discussion summary: the real-world efficacy of hints is mediated by how learners interact with them, the negative associations are not artifacts of prior knowledge, and freely available hints in their common implementation were associated with strategies that bypassed the necessary cognitive effort.
quotes: This study identified two unproductive hint-use behav- iors—requesting hints prematurely and reading them super- ficially—that were consistently and significantly correlated with reduced learning gains across multiple semesters and student cohorts. These findings contribute robust, replicated correlational evidence that refines our understanding of hint usage in digital learning environments. While the theoretical value of hints is well-established, our results underscore that the real-world efficacy of hints is mediated by how learners interact with the provided supports. The negative associations were not merely artifacts of prior knowledge; as these unproductive behaviors remained significantly negatively associated with learning gains even after controlling for pretest scores. This pattern suggests that freely available hints, in their common implementation, were associated with undesired learning strategies that bypassed the essential cognitive effort required for robust learning

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) Results, the scaffold degraded into a shortcut — The authors' mechanism: students bypass the content of the earlier hints to reach the bottom-out answer and enter it without the problem-structuring, concept application and strategy work that produce learning, which degrades the hint system from a scaffold into a shortcut.
quotes: This pattern of rapid hint reading—more frequently observed among learners with lower prior knowledge, and remaining asso- ciated with poorer learning gains even after controlling for prior knowledge—is particularly concerning. It suggests that students may be strategically bypassing the learning content in earlier hints to quickly reach the bottom-out hints, which provide the final answer or direct solution steps. Students employing this gaming strategy can then simply enter the solution without engaging in the cognitive processes necessary for learning, such as understanding the problem structure, applying concepts, or developing solution strategies. This behavior effectively degrades the hint system from a scaffold for learning into a shortcut to answers, undermining its intended pedagogical benefits and potentially explaining the strong negative correlation with learning outcomes observed in our analyses

rows.value: (PDF p. 4) Method, the tests and the counterbalancing — Learning was measured by a pretest, an immediate posttest and a one-week delayed posttest, in three counterbalanced versions randomly assigned across the six possible orders, each of 43 items scored out of 52 points.
quotes: To assess learning outcomes, students completed three decimal tests (pretest, immediate posttest, and one-week delayed posttest) administered during regularly scheduled class time. A key method- ological feature was the use of three counterbalanced test versions (A, B, and C). Each student was randomly assigned one of the six possible sequences of the three tests (e.g., A-B-C, B-C-A, C-A-B, etc.), ensuring that every student took each version once and that each version appeared equally often at each testing occasion. This design aimed to mitigate potential biases, attributing differences in learning outcomes to the intervention rather than to variations in assessment difficulty or practice effects from the pretest. Each test consisted of 43 items, some with multiple components, for a total possible score of 52 points

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Limitations, the correlational ceiling — The obvious rival explanation is that struggling students both ask for more help and learn less, and the pretest control weakens it without removing it, because a single prior-knowledge score cannot absorb motivation, reading fluency or disengagement. There is no manipulation of hint availability anywhere in the paper, so nothing here shows that removing or delaying hints would raise scores. The right reading is that unproductive use marks a bad trajectory, not that hints cause it.
quotes: Several limitations of our study should be noted. First, while our findings for RQ2 show consistent associations between unproduc- tive hint behaviors and learning outcomes, we emphasize that these are correlational relationships from observational data and do not establish causation. The direction of these relationships and poten- tial confounding factors should be investigated in future experimen- tal studies

rows.value: low · The associations themselves are about as solid as observational evidence gets: three independent cohorts, 999 students, eighteen coefficients all negative and all significant, and the pattern holds on a delayed test taken away from the system. The uncertainty is entirely about what causes what, and the authors do not claim more than association.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The students who take the shortcut are the students the help exists for. Prior knowledge correlates with premature requests at -0.567 to -0.697 and with superficial reading at -0.656 to -0.744, the quartile tests are significant in both cases, and the box plots show the bottom quartile far above the other three on both counts. So the same feature is used differently by the top and the bottom of the class, and the way the bottom uses it predicts their worst outcomes. That is a distributional claim about support that a review should carry: an aid can raise a mean and still leave the weakest further behind, because uptake is not uniform and the cheapest way to use it is the least useful. Two cautions. The widening itself is not measured; no gap statistic is reported and no interaction between prior knowledge and behaviour is fitted, so the abstract's claim that the associations are particularly pronounced among lower-knowledge learners rests on the frequency difference, not on a moderation test. And with no no-hint comparison, the counterfactual gap is unknown.

rows.value: Because unproductive hint use is disproportionately concentrated among lower-prior-knowledge students and remains independently associated with poorer outcomes, freely available hints may permit behavioral patterns that widen, rather than reduce, performance gaps among learners.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The paper's most portable idea, and it moves the fault off the learner. The content of the hints was fine and pedagogically graded; what failed was delivery. A persistent, salient button announces that help is always available, and the ladder behind it ends in a level that states the answer, so a user who takes the shortest path converts a problem-solving task into a copying task without breaking any rule. The authors draw the two screenshots side by side to make the point that for such a user the designed interface and an interface that simply prints the answer are the same interface. That shape is not specific to tutoring systems. Any support whose final rung is the finished product, reachable at no cost and at any moment, has it: the completion that writes the function, the assistant that returns the draft, the solver that shows the steps. It reframes what a designer of support is choosing. Not how good the help is, but what it costs to reach the end of it, and whether reaching the end can be made to depend on what the person has already done. This is an argument, not a result: no version of the interface without the button was tested.

rows.value: Consider a learner who, immediately upon receiving any math problem, clicks through all available hints to view the final solution. For this learner, the learning system interface with a hint button as shown in Fig. 6a effectively becomes the design shown in Fig. 6b, in which the final answer is revealed at the very beginning of every problem. This undesirably transforms the learning task into a simple copying exercise... the two unproductive behaviors we identified are not merely instances of poor help-seeking on the learners' end. Rather, they are systematic consequences of an affordance that conflicts with pedagogical goals.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: A requirement named and left unbuilt, with the failure of the obvious version already on record. The paper states the contingency principle in its strong form, that scaffolding should depend on demonstrated effort, diagnoses the button as giving unmediated access, and then puts the remedy in future work: gate the bottom-out hint behind a minimum time or number of attempts. In the same paragraph it concedes that interventions which regulate help-seeking have improved the behaviour without moving domain learning, so the cheap version of contingency is already known to buy compliance rather than understanding. The gap it leaves is precise and worth carrying: making help harder to reach is not the same as making its use cognitively demanding, and only the second is what the theory asks for. The lineage half is worth recording too. This paper does cite the tradition, unlike much recent work that uses the word alone, but a folded whole-text count gives scaffold 11, zone of proximal development 3, contingen 1, and fading, withdraw, gradual, temporar and removal all zero. Even here, the operational half of scaffolding, that support is meant to be taken away, never appears.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The method is the reusable part, and it is almost free. Premature request means the first learner action on a problem instance, after tutor initialization is discarded, was a hint request rather than an attempt. Superficial reading means the gap to the next hint request was shorter than the hint's word count divided by four words a second. Both need nothing but a timestamped event log, which is why the authors position them against the machine-learned gaming detectors built from 24 to 40 engineered features per action, whose transfer across cohorts is unreliable. For a review of supports this is a template: if you want to know whether help is being consumed or used, two order-and-timing rules over ordinary telemetry will tell you something, and will replicate. The validity caveats are real and the authors name two. Four words a second is a population benchmark, so fast readers are miscounted and a slow deliberate reader is scored as careful whatever they took from the hint; and bottom-out hints can be used well, as worked examples, by students who already know a lot. Neither indicator was checked against any independent evidence of what the student was doing.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The reason the study exists, and a methodological point worth more than the effect size it undercuts. The tutor produces a reliable pre-to-post gain with a large effect size, and the average gain is 2.71 points on a 52-point test against a standard deviation of 6.39, so a substantial share of students did not improve or got worse while the mean climbed. Retention is uneven too: one cohort's delayed gain was 1.02 points with a standard deviation of 8.39 and its post-to-delayed change was negative and not significant, while another cohort gained 5.31. A review of supports should take the general form of this: an aggregate effect answers whether a support helps on average and says nothing about whom it helped, and the interesting question, who walked away worse, is invisible unless someone looks at the spread. These authors looked, and what they found in the logs is the rest of this card.

cards.title: Improving Steering and Verification in AI-Assisted Data Analysis with Interactive Task Decomposition

rows.value: S2BW-BDB6148FC855DA6583F6E32F

framework or design space, primary empirical, design principle, failure or counterevidence

The paper takes task decomposition, which LLM systems already perform internally through chain-of-thought and ReAct prompting, and makes it the interface: the model's assumptions and plan become structured editable objects, so a person steers by correcting what the model assumed rather than by rewriting a prompt. A within-subjects comparison against a chat baseline found significantly greater felt control and easier intervention and verification, and no difference in task success, completion time, or hints needed, with the more heavily structured of the two variants also significantly increasing felt information overload.

low · Claims and counterclaims come from one well-reported study whose null results the authors publish alongside its significant ones. cards.title: Ironies of Generative AI: Understanding and Mitigating Productivity Loss in Human-AI Interaction

rows.value: other
review or meta analysis, lineage or history, concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, failure or counterevidence

A 2024 narrative review from Microsoft Research and two universities that reads recent generative-AI user studies against thirty years of Human Factors work on automation and finds the same four failures. Bainbridge's 1983 ironies supply the frame: the more capable the automation, the more the human matters. The four are a shift from producing output to evaluating it, workflows restructured by the new tasks of prompting and repairing output, interruptions from unsolicited suggestions, and task-complexity polarization, the authors' rename of clumsy automation, in which easy tasks get easier and hard ones get harder. The last is the one to carry. Copilot was most useful on boilerplate and microtasks, but decomposing a problem into microtasks was itself the demanding part and the tool could not help with it, and it produced more task failures on medium and hard tasks. Two further results matter for a review of semantic support. Support shaped as feedback or guidance beat support shaped as generated content in three writing studies, where generated text anchored experts and novices alike and lowered quality. And the same suggestion helped or harmed by the moment it arrived, breaking flow during acceleration and helping during exploration. Five Human Factors design directions are offered as remedies and the authors say none has been tested here. Two limits bound everything: the search deliberately selected for productivity losses, so there is no base rate, and the authors explicitly set aside deskilling, calling reduced opportunity for skill development too early to observe as of January 2024.

medium · The four challenges are each supported by several independent studies, the quotations are specific, and the Human Factors precedent for each is named and dated, so what the paper claims and where it got it are not in doubt. Four things bound the whole card. It is a narrative review that says of itself that the search was not systematic or exhaustive. Articles were selected because they reported productivity losses, so nothing here is a base rate. Almost all the generative-AI evidence is qualitative report from studies of four to fifty participants, with one head-to-head comparison and a handful of measured outcomes. And the design half is explicitly untested. Add that several authors work for the company that makes the running example, and the diagnosis should be cited with more confidence than the prescription.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the claim the rest of the paper hangs on, and it is worth carrying in the authors' own terms rather than as a general worry about automation. The person keeps the responsibility and loses the access. Under manual work the picture of the material is a by-product of making it, which is what lets someone say where a fault probably is before looking; a generated artefact arrives without that by-product, so the same judgement now costs a deliberate reconstruction. The Copilot comparison is the cleanest number in the review: against ordinary autocomplete, users failed to finish more often and were no faster when they did. Two things keep this honest. The shift is relative, since prompting is production, so the better description is that a layer of evaluation is added rather than that production is replaced. And the review looked for losses, so this is a description of a failure mode and not a base rate.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The most useful thing on this card for a question about how ideas travel between fields, and it is useful in two directions. Forward, it supplies a vocabulary that HCI can borrow whole: ironies of automation, situational awareness, clumsy automation, task allocation, ecological interface design, procedural traps. Backward, it is evidence of a failure to carry a result. Bainbridge published in 1983, Baxter and colleagues asked in 2012 whether the ironies were still going strong at thirty, and in 2023 and 2024 two independent groups reached for the same paper to explain a new tool. A result that has to be rediscovered at every technology transition is a result the field never held. Note what the paper keeps and what it drops: it takes four of Bainbridge's challenges and sets aside the fifth, deskilling, which is the one that would take longest to show.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.small: concept or lineage, effect, condition, failure
items.lead: The finding this review is worth citing for. Stated at the level of the tool it sounds like a maturity problem that better models will fix. Stated at the level of the work it is structural, and the Barke and Vaithilingam pairing is what shows it: the successful users were the ones who had already decomposed the problem into microtasks, and decomposition is the cognitively expensive step the tool could not support. A support that acts on well-formed units requires the person to have formed the units, which is the part they needed help with. The Human Factors precedent is stronger than a metaphor here, because Metzger and Parasuraman put the freed-resources assumption to a test and it failed twice over: the aid did not lower workload on the demanding tasks, and whatever it freed the controllers could not redirect. Read with the second half, that hard tasks get harder through subtle errors and overwhelming choice, the shape is a support whose benefit falls as the need rises.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The part of the paper that best answers what a support actually does to the shape of the work, and the four pieces are not equally interesting. Prompting and output adaptation as added tasks is now a familiar observation. The loss of task sequence is sharper: a long suggestion made programmers write code before they had an architecture, and prompting made designers specify parameters before they had explored, which is a support inverting the order of the work rather than accelerating it. The loss of feedback is the one a review of meaning-making interfaces should take furthest. What Copilot removed relative to Stack Overflow was not the answer but everything around it, the alternatives, the explanations, the rich social commentary, which is exactly the material that tells a person whether an answer applies to their case. The tool improved the retrieval of answers and removed the means of judging them. Dang's finding belongs beside it: explicit instruction to the system forces writers out of their argument and into the instruction, so the support relocates attention from the object of work to the tool.

rows.value: Automation can restructure workflows in unhelpful ways by introducing new challenging tasks, disrupting familiar task sequences, and removing informative feedback (Figure 1b). This changes what strategies operators use, how they per­ ceive information, and how they act in a specific context, potentially leading to ineffective use of freed-up time and cognitive resources. Thus, rather than reducing what they work on when all or part of tasks are automated, people instead rely on different strategies for working on that task

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The closest thing in this paper to a design principle with a direction, and it runs against the way generative tools are actually built. Three studies, in copywriting, novel writing and inexperienced writing, all found that support which acted on the person's own work beat support which supplied work in its place, and the copywriting study measured a loss rather than merely a smaller gain: generated text anchored the writer and the output got worse. That the anchoring hit experts as hard as novices is what makes it a property of the support rather than of the user. For a review that has to distinguish supports which leave the person holding the meaning from supports which hand them a finished meaning to accept, this is the cleanest available evidence, and it recurs three times in the paper: as a finding, as a personalisation option, and as advice to offer probing questions rather than suggestions. The limits are real. One outcome measure, two preference reports, and no test outside writing.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The conditional worth carrying out of this paper, because it is not the usual one. Most conditional findings in this literature sort people, by expertise or prior knowledge or critical thinking; this one sorts moments. The same programmer, minutes apart, is helped by a long suggestion while exploring and derailed by it while accelerating. That makes the design problem harder than personalisation, because a profile cannot answer it and only the system's read of the current moment can. Two details sharpen it. Rejection does not recover the cost, and the quoted case is an experienced programmer who stopped writing code he already knew how to write in order to check whether the tool had done better, so the interruption taxes exactly the confident execution it was meant to speed. And the users' own fix was to turn the feature off, which says the current designs get the condition wrong often enough that no support is preferred to badly timed support.

rows.value: That complex code suggestions are the most distracting during “acceleration” and are more helpful during “exploration” (Barke et al., 2023) suggests that their timing is a key factor.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: A design space worth taking as a hypothesis set, and worth citing as one rather than as evidence. Three of the five bear directly on a review of meaning-making support. Ecological interface design, because it says the display should carry the structure of the domain rather than the structure of the model, and its concrete form here is offering the same suggestion at several levels of abstraction at once so the person enters where they choose. Task allocation, because making the division of labour explicit and moveable is the direct answer to a support that silently takes the interesting part. And personalising the form of support, which is where the guidance-over-generation result is put to work. The honest reading is that the paper diagnoses with evidence and prescribes without it: the authors say so twice, in section four and again in the conclusion.

items.heading: Claim 8 · CLAIM-008
items.lead: For a review whose question is what support does to the person rather than to the output, this three-sentence exclusion may be the most citable thing in the paper. The authors keep the four ironies about the work and set aside the one about the worker, and the reason they give is not that it does not happen but that it had not yet been studied. That makes this a gap named from inside the literature and dated to January 2024, by six authors including a Microsoft lab director, in a review whose whole method is looking for what the older literature already knew. The older literature already knew this one. It is the one nobody had measured.

cards.title: Embodying an Interactive AI for Dance Through Movement Ideation
cards.meta: 2023 · Creativity and Cognition · doi 10.1145/3591196.3593336 · Route C

rows.value: other
concept or theory, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

Conceptually and methodologically grounded: speculative design is enacted as embodied role-play and bodystorming, reflexive thematic analysis is used to derive themes, and embodied-design and kinaesthetic-creativity work motivates access to tacit bodily knowledge. These foundations support interpretation of practitioner expectations; the paper does not operationalize an embodied-cognition model in an AI system.

medium · All four fit candidates have clear page-grounded support, but the evidence comes from reflexive analysis of two short workshops with six self-selected dancers, primarily analyzed by a non-practitioner lead author, and no actual AI-dancer or downstream outcome was evaluated.

sections.title: 4 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: For semantic support in creative co-action, the transferable mechanism is calibrated continuity plus interpretable deviation: enough shared context to anticipate the partner, with departures that productively reopen the trajectory. This is inferred from human role-play, not demonstrated as an effect of an AI system.

rows.value: Across the bodystorming workshops, participants described predictability from a shared image as supporting co-improvisational flow, while novelty and surprise could redirect an improvisation, inject energy, and help escape creative loops.

pair dance improvisation; movement ideation; embodied speculative workshops; experienced dancers and dance composers represented by the workshop participants; co-creative movement responses combining recognizable continuation with contextually legible deviation; Predictability depends on rapport and an understood shared image between partners. (author stated); Surprise is productive when it changes the shared direction in a way participants can take up and continue. (author stated); The continuity-plus-surprise formulation assumes that a departure remains interpretable within the ongoing activity. (reviewer inferred)

The claim concerns how dancers sustain a recognizable joint trajectory while using surprise to renew or redirect it.; pair improvisation; movement ideation; maintaining and redirecting creative flow; anticipating a partner’s movement; building a shared frame; recovering from creative impasses
not measured · No artifact, process, or learning-or-transfer outcome from an actual AI system was measured; reported changes in flow and energy are qualitative workshop observations.

empirically supported in paper · The mechanism is supported by reflexive thematic analysis of participant discussion and enacted human role-play. Support is qualitative and does not include evaluation of an AI-dancer. · primary empirical, author discussion

The authors deliberately forewent any AI model and used participant role-play. (author stated); The small participant group provides limited perspectives and may not represent other dance communities. (author stated)
(PDF p. 8) Section 4.3, left column, closing paragraph on novelty and creative impasses — Both workshop groups treated novelty as a way to reopen creativity and avoid repetitive loops.
quotes: The concept of novelty was mentioned explicitly by both groups as a crucial part of what their partners can contribute to open “a way out when you are out of creativity”-P1W2 and avoid getting stuck “in a loop”-P3W1.

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Section 5.1, right column, paragraph on surprise changing the shared image — The authors report that surprise can change a shared image, redirect flow, and inject energy into improvisation.

This change in direction, or “flow”, may manifest in various ways, through amount of movement, shifts in dynamics and energy or use of space. When participants are able to surprise each other and change the “shared image” of the improvisation, it injects new energy into the interaction.

This shared image helps the participants predict what their partner might do next and where the improvisation is going.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The field-level lesson is that representational error can function as semantic material when practitioners can translate an alien form through their own bodies; realism is therefore not a universal proxy for creative usefulness. (author stated); The challenge to realism applies to exploratory creative usefulness, not necessarily to tasks where faithful replication is the objective. (reviewer inferred)

An AI-dancer’s lack of a body and sensory experience could also produce difficulty relating to it and a sense akin to alienation. (author stated); The study used human role-play rather than generated movement from an AI model. (author stated); The interpretation is based on a small participant group with limited perspectives. (author stated)

(PDF p. 5) Section 4.1, right column, paragraph on impossible movements and bodily translation — Participants could treat physically impossible movement as material for bodily translation and inspiration.
quotes: Some of the mistakes the AI-dancer makes may break with what is possible for a human, such as limbs growing or shrinking and distorting into strange angles and shapes. As the participants point out, this does not need to be a hindrance, instead, it can invite the dancer to attempt to translate these abstract shapes or impossible movements into their bodies: “Even if it is bio-mechanically not possible to produce, we as an artist get a lot of inspiration just by seeing that”-P1W1.

cards.meta: 2023 · Computer Supported Cooperative Work (CSCW) · doi 10.1007/s10606-023-09463-w · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-B82CBE96B0864F3C773FD309
other
design principle, framework or design space, primary empirical, concept or theory

A participatory design method built so that people with acquired brain injuries can hold their own in a design session with their own clinicians, and the mechanism is a card. The designer writes short cue statements from ethnography, in a deliberately incomplete metonymic form, and renders them so the least able participant can use them; patients then discuss and select cards among themselves before ever meeting a professional. What the analysis traces is where each card ended up. Three uses appear. As the only voice, where the patient cannot argue and the professional decides, but the decision still originates in the patient's card. As a discussion partner, in one patient's words helping them make themselves understood in the moment because they can forget. And as a winning argument. Which of the three happens depends on whether the person had actually chosen that card earlier: cards adopted by going along with the group were disowned later, I did not choose this card. The authors also say the honest thing, that they cannot compare any of it against a session without cards.

high · Seven patients and eight clinicians across two workshops at one hospital, with two recordings unusable, analysed by discourse analysis and open coding without a second rater. There is no condition without cards and the authors say so, so every claim about what the cards did is an interpretation of talk in sessions that all had them. What raises this above anecdote is that the unit of analysis is a traceable object: each card can be followed from the statement the designer wrote, through the group that did or did not choose it, to its position on a final storyboard, and the disowned-card finding falls out of that trace rather than out of impressions.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: As literal an instance of the review's subject as this corpus contains. A small external object holds a meaning its owner cannot reliably produce in the moment, and holding it is what lets them take part. The patient says why in one sentence: the cards help them make themselves understood and find the wording, because they can forget. The support is not helping anybody think better; it is standing in for a capacity that fails intermittently. Three modes are distinguished and the weakest is the most interesting. Where the patient could not argue at all and the professional decided, the card still carried the idea into the storyboard, so the support succeeded while the person it supports was silent. That is influence without participation, achieved by an artifact made earlier when the person was able, and nothing else in this corpus describes it. The other two modes, the card as a discussion partner and as a winning argument, are the ordinary ones, and the authors are careful that neither the person nor the card is sufficient alone.

rows.value: The patients used the cards as a partner for better self-articulation. In view of an MACI patient's memory or attention problems, in the absence of the cards the patient might have forgotten what to say or may have been distracted. On the other hand, the card on its own would not represent the patient's ideas to their fullest. So together they form a more powerful gestalt that can be discussed on equal terms with healthcare professionals. Even in cases where the patient's only voice was the cards, their ideas were not lost, and they made a more substantial contribution than would have been possible without the cards.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the finding worth taking out of the paper, and it is nearly an aside. The same physical object works or fails depending on something that happened before the session: whether the person actually argued for it, or merely went along with the group that chose it. Cards the patient had contested were used as partners and as weapons; a card adopted by association produced I did not choose this card, and sat there as a voice its owner disclaimed. So prefabricated support material is not self-sufficient. It works to the extent that the person has already made it theirs, which means the earlier session is not a warm-up but the step that loads the card. Stated for the review: an externalised representation carries only as much of someone's position as they invested in it, and handing somebody a well-made artifact they did not help make gives them something to hold rather than something to say. The authors see the implication and tell future adopters to think about how to promote grounded moves, without saying how.

rows.value: Another phenomenon was that when the card was used as the only voice, the participants who held it distanced themselves from it. When the patient stated I didn't choose this card, we traced this back to the horizontal group session and found that the patient had not chosen the card. The card was selected as a design idea by association with the majority, so the patient did not have an understanding of and connection with the card. A grounded move in the patients' horizontal group session thereby created incentives for patients to use a card as a partner or to win an argument during the vertical group session.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The sequencing is a support in its own right, separable from the cards. Meeting your own kind before meeting the party with more power means arriving with a position that several people have already backed, and the authors describe the whole first stage as preparing the weaker group. Two things make it more than a facilitation trick. It converts an individual's tentative idea into a group's position, so the argument the person carries into the encounter is not only theirs, which is exactly the mechanism CLAIM-002 shows determines whether the artifact works. And the authors position it against something that normally takes time, the design-decision competence a participant develops through repeated mutual learning, saying the prepared representations supply some of the same immediately. Read that way the staging is a shortcut through an apprenticeship. What it leaves open is whether anything transfers past the session, which the paper does not ask.

rows.value: PD sessions with parallel horizontal groups, people that belong to the same user group, to move statements to design ideas; PD sessions with vertical groups, compounded by people who belong to different user groups, to bring design ideas to the representation of the final design outcomes. Through the cards in the first phase and by encouraging the group design ideas to move in the horizontal session, the designer/researcher is thus preparing the weaker group to go to the vertical session with some power to discuss and contribute equally to the final design outcome.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: An equity rule with teeth, because it works by removing an advantage rather than by adding a compensation. Everyone gets the same restricted representational form, pitched at what the least able participant can use, so fluency in the usual medium stops counting. The effect is on the stronger party's expression as much as on the weaker one's, which is what distinguishes this from the more common move of giving the disadvantaged participant extra help. The warrant is inherited and specific: prior work found that the ability to create a representation is what drives power in co-design, so the design lever is the representation rather than the talk. Note the scope condition the authors attach, that the method does not cover a group who cannot represent themselves in the cooperative work at all. That places it in the band where capacity is intermittent rather than absent, which is exactly the band where an external representation can substitute for it.

rows.value: Define design statement representation options that are adapted to the representation abilities of the most vulnerable group involved in the cooperative relationship. Enabling stakeholders to generate design ideas and standardising the representation in a way that is adapted to the weaker group gives all of the stakeholders equal opportunities to envision future solutions and to represent the ideas in a simple way, thereby equilibrating their opportunities and increasing the weaker user group's power to influence the design outcome.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The power the method redistributes does not disappear; it moves to whoever writes the cards. The authors say so plainly, which is rarer than it should be in this literature, and their three countermeasures are worth recording as the honest state of the art. Keep the statements deliberately incomplete, using a metonymic form that recalls an episode without describing it, so the person has something to think from rather than something to agree with. Put a domain expert who is not a stakeholder in the loop as a check against leading. And tell participants out loud that the material is unfinished and can be rejected. The evidence that this worked is thin and interesting: patients realised early that the cards were only general ideas, and their later interpretations were evolved versions rather than repetitions, more detailed than the statement they started from. That is the right test to have reached for. It is reported without counts and against no alternative wording, so it establishes that the authors were watching for the problem rather than that they solved it.

cards.title: Surfacing AI Explainability in Enterprise Product Visual Design to Address User Tech Proficiency Differences

rows.value: S2W-1EA42FC3E2B7F97D8B5FF98B
other
primary empirical, design principle, failure or counterevidence

A three-phase industrial case study on an enterprise churn-prediction dashboard, in front of the people who actually use such things and have no data scientist to ask. In the first phase fifteen professionals were shown the shipped design; five could not say which customers to target, three produced a confident recommendation from a misreading, and the model quality indicator, a letter grade in a green circle, was read by four as meaning the model made no errors and by six as not being a grade at all, most of them educated outside the country whose grading scale it borrowed. Trust, meanwhile, sat at the top of the scale in people who had just described a chart as showing something it did not show, with the least technical saying they trusted machine output over human because data never lies. A mixed expert workshop then produced two redesigns whose changes are unglamorous: axis labels, an ordering by magnitude, a sentence of plain language on hover for every element, a numeric accuracy score with an explicit scale replacing the grade, whole numbers chosen specifically to curb over-reliance, and a deeper explanation panel that opens over the dashboard rather than navigating away. In the third phase two of eighteen could not make a recommendation, one of nine misread the chart that had defeated most people before, and the least technical group performed like the most. Trust stayed at ceiling throughout, which is the paper's own uncomfortable point: it moved understanding without moving trust, because trust was never tracking understanding.

medium · Read the direction as reliable and the size as unestablished. This is a case study by the team that owns the product, reported qualitatively at extended-abstract length, with about twenty people per phase and no overlap between them. What makes it worth its weight is that the outcome is an act rather than a rating, that the design changes are enumerated precisely enough to reuse, and that the two most useful findings are failures the authors report against their own product.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Two distinct failures in one small design decision, and both generalise. The first is that compressing a quality measure into a grade removes the room in which uncertainty lives, so people read it as a guarantee; the paper's own fix, whole numbers on an explicit scale, is a rare instance of a design move made specifically against over-reliance and named as such. The second is rarer in this literature and worth carrying on its own: a semantic token can be legible only to people educated in one place, and it fails silently, because a familiar-looking symbol invites a reading rather than a question. Six of fifteen did not know they were looking at a grade.

rows.value: The letter-grade performance chart was easily misread, contained a socioculturally specific design, and did not allow effective understanding of uncertainty: four participants took the green ring around the A to mean the model had no error, and six did not read it as a grade at all. To avoid over-reliance and misinterpretation due to sociocultural differences, model performance should be shown as a numerical score with an explicit scale.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: Recorded for the diagnosis rather than the remedy. The guidelines this literature keeps citing tell a team to make the system's capability clear and say nothing about what that looks like on a chart, and a case study is where the translation actually happens. The division of labour the authors report is the interesting part: the data scientist attended to model performance, the content designer to wording, and someone to what the person is prompted to do next, which is a decomposition of explainability into the roles that own each piece of it. cards.title: Who Should I Trust: AI or Myself? Leveraging Human and AI Correctness Likelihood to Promote Appropriate Trust in AI-Assisted Decision-Making

rows.value: other
framework or design space, design principle, primary empirical, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper is conceptually grounded in trust calibration and mental-model research and operationalizes similarity-based judgment, anchoring, and cognitive forcing in a two-stage architecture: estimate task-instance human capability, then adapt the information and sequence through which human and AI decisions are combined.

medium · The complete article provides direct methods, quantitative results, qualitative feedback, and explicit limitations. quotes: Participants in Adaptive Workflow and Adaptive Recommendation were forced to think independently. quotes: Exploiting knowledge complementarity is beneficial for team performance. Our study found that although the team performance in the proposed three conditions exceeded AI Only and Human Only, the improvement was not “remarkable” (about 3-4%). cards.title: The "Active Search" Hypothesis: How Search Strategies Relate to Creative Learning
cards.meta: 2021 · Proceedings of the 2021 Conference on Human Information Interaction and Retrieval · doi 10.1145/3406522.3446046 · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-5D4B1DD855B1269FAF314AEB
other
primary empirical, measurement or method, failure or counterevidence, design principle

A five-page CHIIR 2021 study: 34 undergraduate designers, 30 minutes of web search on a transport brief, a browser plugin logging queries and pages, and pre- and post-task summaries and problem statements scored for learning. Part of the contribution is an instrument. Creative learning is made measurable by borrowing Anderson and Krathwohl's cognitive levels from education, Wilson and Wilson's summary-scoring measures from information science, and Abdulla and Cramond's five-level problem-finding hierarchy from creativity research, each with a reported inter-rater kappa between 0.58 and 0.74. The findings run two ways. What people wanted was not lookup: 22 wanted to get oriented in an unfamiliar space, 27 wanted patterns and criteria, 21 wanted inspiration, and the paper says plainly that this goes beyond what search tools are optimised for. What stopped them was articulation, not retrieval: 29 of 34 could not turn an ill-defined need into a query, 12 lacked the domain vocabulary, and 10 could not judge usefulness and fell back on rank position and citation frequency as credibility signals. The headline is that more, longer and more diverse queries go with larger gains on every learning measure. The sharper thing is in the table and unstated: opening more web pages predicts the shallowest outcome only and predicts none of interpretation, critique or problem framing. The authors disclaim causality themselves. Two printed p values are 1.20, and one correlation called significant is 0.18 at a sample of 34.

high · The qualitative half of this paper is well grounded: three information goals and three barriers, each with a count out of 34, coded from open-ended survey responses and triangulated in places against the logs. The quantitative half is where the trouble is. The design is correlational at n equal to 34, the authors name aptitude as a competing explanation they cannot rule out and call the finding a hypothesis in the title, the pooled active searching construct behaves inconsistently across its four components, the instrument's weakest inter-rater agreement attaches to the measure carrying the most significant results, and two of the sixteen printed p values are impossible while one correlation reported as significant is 0.18 at that sample size. What survives strongly is the diagnosis, the instrument and the unstated dissociation between querying and page-opening. What does not survive as stated is the headline correlation table.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.small: concept or lineage, condition, open question
items.lead: The mismatch is between what the tool is built to answer and what the task actually asks. All three goals the study recovers are synthesis goals rather than lookups: 22 participants wanted to get oriented in a space they did not have the concepts for, 27 wanted to find patterns and criteria across sources by comparing and contrasting them, and 21 wanted inspiration for ideas they could not yet name. A ranked list of documents is the wrong shape of answer for all three, and the paper says so directly. For a review of computational support for intellectual work this is a clean statement of a supply-and-demand gap at the level of the task rather than the interface: the dominant support tool for early-stage design work is optimised for a class of request that early-stage design work rarely makes. The counts come from thematic analysis of a post-task survey with 34 respondents, so they show what people said they were doing, not a frequency in the population.

rows.value: We find that searchers have cognitively-complex information goals during early-stage design - goals that go beyond the recall and lookup tasks that current search tools are optimized to fulfill. Additional information goals included wanting to discover design patterns and criteria, and seek inspiration to generate hypotheses and ideas.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Twenty-nine of thirty-four is the number to carry, and it locates the bottleneck before the system is given anything to work with. The interface demands a query; the person has an ill-defined need; the hardest step is the translation between them, and no amount of retrieval quality helps with it. The second barrier is circular in a way the logs capture: a participant could not search for a concept until an article happened to give them the word for it, and then used that word across seven consecutive queries. Acquiring the term is itself an outcome of searching that the interface does not treat as one, and it gates everything after it. The strategies people improvised are legible in the logs and are all workarounds for the same problem: start broad and add terms, one participant issuing seven successive queries that grow from a single word to a place, a source type and a constraint; or ask the question in natural language and hope. Both make queries longer, which is exactly the behaviour the paper's headline finding then correlates with better outcomes, so the strategy and the measure are entangled.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The headline holds in the direction claimed, but the table contains a dissociation the paper never states and it is the more useful finding. Number of unique web pages opened is significant for one outcome only, quality of facts, at an odds ratio of 1.04. For interpretation, critique and problem definition its odds ratios are 0.75, 0.96 and 0.75, all non-significant and two of them below one. Query behaviour, by contrast, predicts the higher rungs: length and diversity carry critique, and number, length and diversity all carry problem definition. So reading more pages tracks only how many good facts you end up with, while varying how you ask tracks whether you can interpret, criticise and frame. If that survives replication it is a conditional a design space can use: the intervention that helps is one that widens the query, not one that surfaces more documents. Two cautions. The authors disclaim causality themselves and the alternative they name is the right one, since a student who can already frame a problem will also know how to vary a query, and the correlation is what either story predicts. And the paper's own reported strategy for coping with the articulation barrier, adding terms and asking questions, produces longer queries, so the predictor is partly a trace of the difficulty rather than of a skill.

rows.value: Overall, we observe that more active, diverse searching (as shown by issuing more, longer, and diverse queries, and opening more web pages) generally corresponds to higher increases in creative learning outcomes (such as gathering more facts, articulating deeper insights, and framing more well-defined problems). We observed significant relationships between active searching behavior and creative learning outcomes, however, we cannot make any causal claims.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Ten of thirty-four said they could not judge whether what they found was useful, and the two heuristics the paper prints as their solutions are both readings of the ranking rather than of the source. One treats being cited often as reliability; the other treats appearing top across several queries as both relevance and trustworthiness. The system supplies an ordering computed for relevance, and the person consumes it as a warrant for truth. That is a failure of the support rather than of the person: nothing in the interface distinguishes the two, and the searcher has no domain knowledge to check against, which is the same deficit that produced the vocabulary barrier. It matters for a review of intellectual support because it is a case where the tool's output is legible enough to be used and not legible enough to be used correctly, and where the substitution goes unnoticed by the user. The paper reports it as a challenge and a strategy and does not name it as a risk; nothing downstream tests whether the heuristic led anyone astray.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The instrument is the part of this paper most likely to outlive it. Creative learning is made measurable by borrowing from three fields at once: the cognitive ladder from education by way of the Search-as-Learning community, three summary-scoring measures from information science for the middle rungs, and a five-level problem-finding hierarchy from creativity research for the top rung. Each carries a reported Fleiss kappa, between 0.58 and 0.74. The substitution at the top is the move that matters. The create level is scored not as ideas produced but as how well-defined a problem statement is, which makes framing rather than generation the creative outcome and is what lets a 30-minute search session be scored for creativity at all. That is a translation worth recording in its own right, and it comes with a cost: the whole construct is measured from written summaries, so what is scored is what a person can articulate in 200 words, not what they understood. One weakness to carry with it. The lowest of the three agreement figures, 0.58 for interpretation of facts, attaches to the measure that produced the most significant results and is the only one below the conventional threshold for moderate agreement.

Early stages of a design process require the designer to learn about a new domain, and involve all these types of learning: from recalling facts (remember) to synthesizing information to discover insights (understand, analyze, evaluate), and asking questions and posing problems in a fruitful and radical ways, generating ideas (create), etc.

Level 1: Problem Discovery: the prob- lem statement is very ill-defined or defined very similar to the given problem. There is no relevant information and no insight to build on. Level 2: Problem Formulation: the problem statement is yet to specify the problem, however, there is enough information that they could discover insights from. Level 3: Problem Construction: the problem statement includes some background information, but the problem finder needs to further evaluate the information to specify a well-informed and well-reasoned problem. Level 4: Problem Iden- tification: the problem statement includes some information and has some preliminary insights about the problem; however, there is no specific problem identified or the problem identified is still rather vague. Level 5: Problem Definition: (most well-defined stage of problem finding) the problem statement identifies as specific, well-informed and well-reasoned problem. items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The printed statistics do not survive checking, in two separate ways, and both are visible on the page. Two of the sixteen p cells in Table 3 are printed as 1.20, which is not a possible p value. And Table 2 is internally inconsistent at n equal to 34: a correlation of 0.18 is marked significant at p equal to 0.04, where the critical value at that sample size is about 0.34, so its true p is near 0.3; while 0.65 is reported at p equal to 0.02, where it would in fact be far smaller. Bonferroni correction, which the paper says it applied throughout, moves p upward, so it cannot rescue the first case and makes it worse. This does not overturn the paper's direction, which is supported by the regressions and by three of the four correlations, but it does mean that one specific headline component, query diversity predicting fact gain, has no valid support in Table 2 at all. Record the finding with the defect attached, because a later synthesis quoting r equal to 0.18 as a significant relationship would be repeating an arithmetic error rather than a result.

cards.title: Scaffolding complex learning: The mechanisms of structuring and problematizing student work
cards.meta: 2018 · Scaffolding · doi 10.1207/s15327809jls1303_2 · Route B · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-76DA9EDC1E1CD8FA2205B667
other
concept or theory, lineage or history, framework or design space, design principle, failure or counterevidence

The paper conceptually extends traditional human scaffolding into software-mediated learning. It grounds scaffolding in Wood, Bruner, and Ross, Vygotsky's zone of proximal development, and cognitive apprenticeship, then uses distributed cognition and Norman's cognitive-artifact account to explain how interface representations transform tasks. Its central synthesis distinguishes two complementary mechanisms—structuring work and problematizing disciplinary content—and develops their design tensions and system-level conditions. The argument is illustrated with prior classroom design research rather than tested through a new controlled evaluation.

medium · The paper states and grounds its mechanisms, lineage, tensions, and system conditions clearly, and it supplies concrete classroom examples. However, it is primarily a theoretical synthesis of prior design research rather than a new controlled evaluation, so process, learning, transfer, and causal effect claims remain unmeasured in this paper.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CL-01-LEARNING-CRITERION
items.lead: This establishes a transfer-sensitive boundary between immediate performance assistance and educational scaffolding. The distinction is conceptually important, but this paper does not itself measure later independent performance or transfer.

(PDF p. 3) Introduction, opening discussion of scaffolding and cognitive apprenticeship — Wood, Bruner, and Ross ground the traditional definition of scaffolding as knowledgeable assistance for otherwise out-of-reach tasks.
quotes: Researchers have invoked the notion of scaffolding, a construct originally crafted to characterize how more experienced peers or adults can assist learners. As defined and used in early research, scaffolding is said to occur when a more knowledgeable person helps a learner succeed in tasks that would be otherwise beyond their reach (Wood, Bruner, & Ross, 1976). In the last two decades of learning sciences research, scaffolding has become increasingly prominent. Scaffolding is a key strategy in cognitive apprenticeship, in which students can learn by taking increasing responsibility and ownership for their role in complex problem solving with the structure and guidance of more knowledgeable mentors or teachers (Collins, Brown, & Newman, 1989).

items.heading: Claim 2 · CL-02-REPRESENTATIONAL-STRUCTURING
items.lead: Representational structuring redistributes cognitive and process work across learner and tool. Its mechanism is not merely adding instructions: the interface externalizes task organization, narrows action possibilities, and makes selected goals or relations salient.

rows.value: Because cognitive artifacts help define and transform tasks, instructional designers can shape representations to support learning. Structuring scaffolds reduce complexity and choice through workspaces, constraints, and prompts that support decomposition, organization, direction, and attention to important goals.
