(PDF p. 9) How Can Tools Help Learners?, opening paragraph — Tool structure changes interaction with a task and what learners can accomplish.
quotes: In considering how to design effective scaffolded tools, it is important to reconceptualize the learning problem from that of an individual working on tasks, perhaps with assistance of another more knowledgeable person, to a consideration of the context in which the people are acting, the tools they use, and the knowledge embedded in this context. Rather than considering what the individual can accomplish, this view of distributed cognition focuses on what a person or group working with tools can accomplish as a system (Hollan, Hutchins, & Kirsh, 2000). The structure of a tool shapes how people interact with the task and affects what can be accomplished.

rows.value: (PDF p. 10) Tools Can Transform Tasks, opening paragraph — Norman's cognitive-artifact construct supplies the account of representations as task-transforming tools.
quotes: Norman (1991) described cognitive artifacts, or tools that are used to represent and manipulate information in a task. Cognitive artifacts can change the task in fundamental ways.

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Tools Can Transform Tasks, concluding paragraph — Designers can bend interface representations toward instructional purposes and thereby shape how learners think about tasks.
quotes: In the design of scaffolded tools, instructional designers can use this mapping to an advantage. Rather than striving only for transparency between the representation and the world it represents, designers can bend that representation to instructional purposes. Cognitive artifacts provide a lever for designers to shape how learners think about tasks.

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Mechanisms of Scaffolding: Structure and Problematize, concluding paragraph — The author identifies structuring and problematizing as complementary software-scaffolding mechanisms.
quotes: I propose two complementary mechanisms of scaffolding in software tools—it can help structure the task of problem solving, and it can problematize subject matter, and thus provoke learners to devote resources to issues they might not otherwise address.

items.lead: Semantically constrained artifacts can act as forcing functions for epistemic work: they turn tacit interpretations into inspectable choices and shared inscriptions, creating occasions for articulation, negotiation, and disciplinary sensemaking. items.heading: Claim 4 · CL-04-BALANCE-AND-CONTINGENCY
items.lead: Scaffolding quality depends on contingent calibration between tractability and productive disciplinary complexity. Static or learner-controlled interface scaffolds approximate this calibration less closely than an expert human who diagnoses learner state and tailors assistance.

rows.value: Structuring and problematizing are complementary but potentially conflicting. Overwhelming complexity can defeat productive engagement, while excessive simplification can produce lockstep activity without target reasoning. Effective balance depends on learners recognizing the encoded distinctions, yet most scaffolded tools have limited capacity to individualize support to learner state.

cards.title: Promoting Self-Explanation to Improve Mathematics Learning: A Meta-Analysis and Instructional Design Principles

review or meta analysis, design principle, failure or counterevidence, concept or theory

A meta-analysis of 26 published mathematics experiments that pitted prompts to explain against an unprompted control, and it is one of the few places in this corpus that measures what is left after the support stops. Every outcome is a knowledge test taken once the prompting phase is over. Immediately after, the pooled gains are small to moderate and all clear zero: procedural knowledge 0.28 over 19 experiments, conceptual knowledge 0.33 over 16, procedural transfer 0.46 over 9. After a delay of one week to one month, only nine experiments ever looked, and only transfer survives at 0.32 with an interval starting at 0.02; procedural knowledge falls to 0.13 and conceptual knowledge to minus 0.05, both far from significant. The average also hides its opposite: true heterogeneity of 62 to 73 per cent, and single studies from minus 0.77 to 1.31. Two moderators are tested. Controlling time on task changes nothing, which the authors read as evidence the effect is a process and not extra minutes. Scaffolding the explanation itself, by training beforehand or by making the response a fill-in or a menu choice, raises the conceptual effect and nothing else. Four design guidelines follow. The paper is candid that classroom evidence is thin, seven experiments, four of them inside computer tutors, and it names fading as future work rather than findings.

medium · The reporting is unusually honest for a meta-analysis: the authors give the dispersion, decline to pool what cannot be pooled, and repeat the classroom and delay limits in the abstract, the results and the conclusion. The immediate effects and the heterogeneity are firm. Three things hold the card back from a low rating. N counts experiments and the paper reports no participant totals at all, so the precision behind 0.28 or 0.32 cannot be judged from this document. The delayed estimates rest on six or seven experiments each, and the one that survives clears zero by 0.02. And the moderator codes for scaffolding and time on task were partly assigned by the authors' judgement where studies did not report the information. Only published work was searched, which the authors say may inflate the ratio of positive effects to non-effects, so the negative cases in the table are probably an undercount.

sections.title: 8 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The central positive result, and it is measured in the condition this review cares about: the prompts operate during learning and the test comes afterwards, so the numbers describe what the learner can do once the support has stopped. Three pooled effects, each a standardized mean difference against a no-prompted-explanation control, all with intervals clearing zero: procedural knowledge 0.28 over 19 experiments with 95 per cent interval 0.07 to 0.49, conceptual knowledge 0.33 over 16 experiments with 0.09 to 0.57, procedural transfer 0.46 over 9 experiments with 0.16 to 0.76. The ordering matters as much as the sizes, because the largest effect falls on the measure furthest from the trained task, which is what the authors' generalization mechanism predicts and the opposite of what a rehearsal account would predict. Two cautions belong with the numbers and both are the authors' own. N counts experiments, not learners, and the paper reports no participant totals anywhere. And the control learners may have explained to themselves unprompted, so 0.28 is what the prompt adds on top of whatever explaining already happened, not the value of explaining.

rows.value: As expected, prompting students to self-explain led to a small to moderate improvement in mathematics learning. In particular, self-explanation prompts promote greater procedural knowledge (ES = 0.28), conceptual knowledge (ES = 0.33) and procedural transfer (ES = 0.46) when knowledge was assessed immediately after the intervention. In line with the mechanisms self-explanation is thought to support—knowledge integration and/or knowledge generalization—the effects were stronger on the measures that required deeper knowledge.

rows.value: low · Three pooled estimates with intervals that clear zero, from a documented search and an explicit coding scheme, and the authors report the dispersion honestly. What is uncertain is not the direction but the generality: no participant counts, published studies only, and mostly laboratory settings.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the claim the corpus most needs and the one with the least behind it. Of 26 tabulated study entries, nine came back after a delay of one week to one month. What survived is the transfer effect, 0.32 over six experiments, z 2.07, interval 0.02 to 0.63, which clears zero by two hundredths. What did not survive is the rest: procedural knowledge drops from 0.28 to 0.13 with an interval from minus 0.13 to 0.39, and conceptual knowledge from 0.33 to minus 0.05 with an interval from minus 0.29 to 0.19. So the answer to whether the change outlasts the support is partly yes and mostly not established, and the two are easy to confuse because the immediate table is fuller and greener. One within-study check helps. Rittle-Johnson 2006 is the only row with all six cells: 0.43, minus 0.12 and 0.41 immediately, then 0.37, minus 0.27 and 0.24 at two weeks. Procedures and transfer decay slightly and stay positive, conceptual knowledge is negative at both horizons. The same shape as the pooled result, from one set of children, which is mild reassurance that the delayed nulls are not an artefact of a different study mix. The authors' own conclusion is that other techniques, such as repeated testing, may be needed for retention.

rows.value: Much less research has investigated whether these effects persist over a delay. Only nine experiments have included a delayed posttest, with the delay ranging from one week to one month. Self-explanation prompts did improve procedural transfer over a delay (ES = 0.32). However, the effect sizes were much lower for procedural knowledge (ES = 0.13) and conceptual knowledge (ES = −0.05) and were far from significant. [...] However, evidence that self-explanation reliably promotes retention of knowledge over a delay or learning within a classroom context is much more limited.

rows.value: medium · The numbers are reported plainly and the authors do not oversell them, but each delayed estimate rests on six or seven experiments and the survival result clears zero by 0.02. The direction of the finding, that transfer outlasts the support while procedure and concept advantages are not shown to, is trustworthy as a description of this evidence and weak as a general claim.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The most useful thing this paper does for a review of supports is refuse to let the average stand alone. All three heterogeneity tests are significant and true heterogeneity accounts for 62 to 73 per cent of the variance, which means the effect of a prompt is a property of the pairing of prompt, content and learner rather than a property of prompting. Table 1 makes the spread concrete. Immediate procedural effects run from Hilbert et al. 2008 at minus 0.77 to Aleven and Koedinger 2002 at 1.31; immediate conceptual from Grosse and Renkl 2006 at minus 0.69 to Hodds et al. 2014 at 1.17. Whole studies land on the wrong side: every one of Mwangi and Sweller's three entries is negative, minus 0.40 immediate procedural and minus 0.72 procedural and minus 0.19 transfer after a delay; Grosse and Renkl 2006 is minus 0.30 procedural and minus 0.69 conceptual; Broers and Imbos 2005 is minus 0.29 conceptual. So the honest reading of CLAIM-001 is that prompting shifts the distribution upward while leaving a real share of cases at or below zero, and that the paper's four guidelines exist precisely because the mean is not the story. Nothing here identifies which cases fail; the two moderators tested account for only part of the spread and the authors do not report how much.

rows.value: Despite the general benefit of self-explanation prompts for immediate learning outcomes, in some studies, self-explanation prompts did not impact learning (as indicated by an effect size near 0, see Table 1) and occasionally even had a negative impact on learning (as indicated by a negative effect size, see Table 1). Indeed, there was substantial heterogeneity of effects Q(18) = 49.38, p < 0.001 for procedural knowledge, Q(15) = 55.33, p < 0.001 for conceptual knowledge, and Q(8) = 21.27, p = 0.006 for procedural transfer), indicating substantial variability in the effect sizes across studies. This heterogeneity was mainly due to true heterogeneity (I2 ranged from 62.4 to 72.9%).

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The design lever, and it is a support on a support: the mathematics is not scaffolded, the act of explaining is. Two forms are coded. Training beforehand means describing and motivating the strategy, modelling it, and practising it. A structured response means filling blanks in a partly written explanation or picking one from a menu or glossary. About half the studies did one or the other. The moderator is outcome-specific and that is the useful part: the conceptual-knowledge effect is larger where explanations were scaffolded, beta 0.67 at p = 0.004, and still larger on the tighter test that drops the training studies and compares structured responses with nothing, beta 0.55 at p = 0.043; transfer at 0.36 with p = 0.273 and procedural knowledge at 0.18 with p = 0.454 do not move. So a designer choosing to constrain the response should expect to buy understanding of the principle, not procedural fluency or generalisation. Two things temper this. Structured formats have been used exclusively inside computer tutors, which also supply accuracy feedback, so the estimate is for the whole package rather than the format. And the largest single negative procedural effect in the table, minus 0.77, comes from a structured-response study. It is also worth recording for lineage that this paper uses the word scaffolding throughout, including in the title of its first guideline, with no citation anywhere to the scaffolding literature.

The effects of scaffolding self-explanation on procedural transfer and procedural knowledge are not reliable, so the advantages of providing scaffolding may be less substantial for promoting those types of knowledge.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The closest thing in the paper to a mechanism test, and it is a null used as evidence. The reasoning is sound in shape: if the benefit were bought with extra minutes, the effect should shrink in the studies that fixed study time, and across all three outcomes it did not move reliably. The reasoning is thin in strength. Three non-significant coefficients over at most 19 experiments is weak support for equality rather than evidence of it, one of the three is a sizeable minus 0.34, and the coding was partly inferred by the authors where studies did not report time on task. The cost the null is arguing about is real and quantified: in one study prompted learners spent about 75 minutes against 45 for the control, so the support asks for two thirds again as much time. And the authors' own study that matched time by giving controls extra problems found the advantage shrank to a few subscales, which sits awkwardly beside the moderator null. What the corpus should take from this is the question, not the answer: whether a support earns its place is a comparison against the best alternative use of the same minutes, and this paper says that comparison has barely been run.

rows.value: First, whether studies controlled for time on task did not influence the effectiveness of explanation prompts for procedural knowledge (β = −0.34, p = 0.145), conceptual knowledge (β = −0.22, p = 0.458), or procedural transfer (β = 0.33, p = 0.304). Thus, the size of the self-explanation effect was not significantly smaller when studies controlled for time on task (e.g., by fixing study time). This is in line with the arguments that self-explanation promotes effective learning processes, not simply more time on task.

items.lead: The most transferable finding in the paper for anyone designing a support that directs attention, and it is a cost measured rather than a cost imagined. A prompt does not add attention, it aims it. The same manipulation raised conceptual knowledge of the domain principles and lowered procedural knowledge, in mathematics and again in a tax law task, and the process trace shows the mechanism plainly: prompted learners performed fewer calculations while studying. The reverse case closes the argument, with procedure-directed prompts harming conceptual knowledge. Table 1 carries the mathematics instance as row 5, minus 0.21 procedural against 0.84 conceptual, which is the trade-off written as two numbers from one study. The implication for a review of supports is a design rule with a price attached: what a prompt names is what gets attended to, and everything it does not name competes for the same budget. The authors' own guideline is to balance attention across all the important content, which is easy to state and, on this evidence, hard to do.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The condition that says when the support is worth adding, and it is a redundancy rule rather than a failure. A prompt is worth what the inferences it elicits are worth, and only when those inferences were not supplied some other way. Teach children the meaning of the equal sign directly and there is nothing left for the prompt to draw out: two experiments with elementary children found no gain on any measure, and Table 1 records one of them as 0.06, minus 0.08 and 0.02 immediately and minus 0.30, minus 0.27 and minus 0.17 after the delay, and the other as minus 0.03, 0.01, 0.05 and 0.10. The authors give the converse boundary themselves, which makes the rule usable: for procedures that are hard to invent, such as fraction division, concept instruction alone will not be enough and the prompt should still earn its place. The same logic explains the comparison with instructional explanations, where learners given ready-made explanations learned about as much as learners prompted to build their own, in these mathematics studies and in a wider meta-analysis, while taking less time. That result is awkward for the paper's own mechanism, since the account says the learner must generate the inference; the authors' reading, that the self-explaining learners had trouble generating correct inferences, effectively concedes that explanation quality and not explanation authorship is the active ingredient.

items.heading: Claim 8 · CLAIM-008
items.lead: The honest boundary on everything above, and the authors put it in their abstract and their conclusion as well as here. Seven of the 26 tabulated study entries ran in a classroom. In those seven the immediate procedural effect is 0.38 at p = 0.08, which does not reach significance, and the conceptual effect is 0.15 at p = 0.56, which is nothing. Transfer and every delayed outcome could not be pooled at all for want of studies. So the two results this paper is best known for, the transfer advantage and its survival over a delay, have no classroom estimate whatsoever. What the seven are matters as much as how many: four ran inside computer tutoring systems and the other three in college classrooms during class or as homework, so there is no estimate at all for ordinary primary or secondary teaching. The three non-computer classroom studies split two to one against, and the one that worked was the one that trained learners to explain first, which is the paper's only cross-check between its scaffolding guideline and its classroom problem. Set beside the authors' own observation that a laboratory experimenter's presence may raise the effort learners put into explaining, and that unmonitored learners may put in less, the gap between 0.46 for transfer in the laboratory and nothing measurable in a school is the most consequential open question the paper leaves.

Four out of the seven experiments conducted in a classroom context were implemented using computer-tutoring systems, and the remaining three were done in college classrooms [...] Thus, evidence that self-explanation prompts can effectively promote mathematics learning and retention in regular primary- or secondary-education classrooms is quite limited.

Future research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of struc- tured response formats on paper-and-pencil assignments, as well as on approaches for transitioning from structured response formats to open-ended response formats

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Sect. 6.1 Classroom context — Two limits should be recorded plainly. The paper reports no participant counts at all: N throughout is a count of experiments, so there is no sample size for the pooled effects in this document. And most of the corpus is laboratory work with an experimenter watching, which the authors themselves say may raise the effort learners put into explaining. Both push the same way. The number that generalises to a classroom is the classroom number, and that one is 0.38 at p = 0.08 for procedures with nothing at all for transfer or retention.
quotes: Although a majority of research on prompted self-explana- tion has been conducted on educationally-relevant content, only seven published experiments on mathematics learning have been conducted in realistic classroom contexts (see Table 1). A majority of research was conducted in a labora- tory context with close supervision of an experimenter. The demand characteristics of a laboratory setting may increase the probability that participants attempt to generate reason- able explanations. In unmonitored settings, learners may put in less effort

rows.value: (PDF p. 8) Sect. 5.1 Guideline 1 — The most effective version of the support is confounded with its delivery medium. Structured response formats are the only scaffold with a reliable moderator effect, and the authors say they have been used exclusively inside computer tutors, which also supply feedback on explanation accuracy. So the estimate for structured responses is an estimate for structured responses plus a tutor plus feedback, and nothing in the paper separates them. The transition from structured to open-ended responses, which is the design question that matters for withdrawal, is listed as future work.
quotes: structured self-explanation response formats have been used exclusively in studies implemented in computer tutors. They may be particularly important as an alternative to typing open-ended explanations. They also facilitate pro- viding feedback on the accuracy of the explanations, which is rarely done when responses are not structured. Future research is needed to evaluate the effectiveness of struc- tured response formats on paper-and-pencil assignments, as well as on approaches for transitioning from structured response formats to open-ended response formats

rows.value: low · The counts and the two subgroup estimates are stated plainly, the authors decline to pool what cannot be pooled, and they repeat the limitation in the abstract, the results and the conclusion. The uncertainty is in the world, not in the reporting: seven experiments, four of them inside computer tutors, is simply too little to say what happens in a classroom.
This card supports reading this paper. It does not establish a cross-paper pattern or effect, a prevalence estimate, or any part of the Stream 1 denominator.

cards.title: Parallel prototyping leads to better design results, more divergence, and increased self-efficacy
cards.meta: 2011 · ACM Trans. Comput.-Hum. Interact. · doi 10.1145/1879831.1879836 · Route C

rows.value: S2CW-3EC16876F1E9F4CF537EFD5C
other
primary empirical, design principle, failure or counterevidence, concept or theory

A between-subjects experiment that holds a semantic support constant and moves only its delivery schedule. Thirty-three people designed web banner ads and received expert critique statements from a fixed fifty-item corpus, either after each of five prototypes or after batches of three and two. Same statements, same amount, same time. The batched condition produced ads that clicked better and rated higher, prototype sets that crowd raters judged more diverse, and novices who ended the session more confident rather than less. Half the serial participants called the neutral critique negative; none of the parallel ones did. The paper explains this through comparison, through Osborn's rule about deferring judgment, and through Bandura's self-efficacy, and turns Tohidi et al.'s finding about candid critics around to ask what alternatives do to the person being criticised. A follow-up shows randomly chosen statements from the same corpus performing worse than no critique at all.

medium · A well-controlled experiment whose central manipulation is exactly the kind this review needs, reported with its own null results left in view. Read the effect directions as reliable and the sizes as provisional: thirty-three participants, one session, one artifact type, several results sitting just under p equals 0.05, and a proposed mechanism that the study's internal correlations do not confirm.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is the cleanest available demonstration that a semantic support is not fully described by its content. The critique statements were drawn from the same fifty-item corpus in both conditions, chosen by the same person, and the total dose was identical. What differed was whether the person held two other versions of their own work when they read it. A review that codes supports by what they say will record these two conditions as the same support, and they are not.

rows.value: Participants who created three prototypes before receiving any critique produced final designs that performed significantly better on click-through, on time spent on the client site and on independent expert ratings than participants who received the same critique after each prototype.
Earlier outline · Work process (now RQ2) · Earlier chapter · Conditional outcomes · S2Q2 · Cumulative design knowledge

an open-ended visual design task with an external client brief; novice and lightly experienced individual designers; expert critique statements delivered on a batch of three prototypes rather than on each one in turn; The result holds under equal prototype counts, equal feedback and equal total time; parallel work bought nothing extra, it only reordered. (author stated); Individuals working alone for a single session on a small visual artifact, with no professional designers among them. (author stated)

Holding the feedback itself constant, giving it on a batch of alternatives rather than on each attempt in turn produced better finished work.; prototyping; receiving a critique; revising a design; extracting a general principle from feedback on specific work
measured

empirically supported in paper · A between-subjects experiment with one manipulated variable, outcomes taken from a live 15-day advertising campaign, from client-site analytics and from seven blind expert raters. · primary empirical

The two quality measures did not agree with each other: click performance was not a predictor of expert rating, and two of the serial condition's worst-rated ads were among the best click performers. (author stated); Thirty-three people, one artifact type, one sitting with a tool none of them had used before. The effect sizes are small and the significance thresholds are at p just under 0.05 on most measures. (reviewer inferred)
(PDF p. 5) Section 3.1, what was held constant — Prototype count, feedback amount and total time were held constant across conditions.
quotes: The study held constant the number of prototypes created, the amount of feedback provided, and the overall time allotted.

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) Section 5, the manipulation restated — The single manipulated variable was when the critique arrived.
quotes: The only difference between conditions was a matter of when participants received a critique on their ideas, after each concept or after multiple creations.

rows.value: (PDF p. 1) Abstract, the performance result — Parallel ads beat serial ads on click-through and on expert ratings.
quotes: As measured by clickthrough data and expert ratings, ads created in the Parallel condition signiﬁcantly outperformed those from the Serial condition.

rows.value: (PDF p. 12) Section 4.1.3, the expert rating result — Independent expert raters scored parallel ads higher.
quotes: Parallel ads were rated higher (μ = 24.4, SD = 9.7) than serial ads (μ = 21.7, SD = 8.8) (F(1,203) = 3.871, p < 0.05)

rows.value: (PDF p. 11) Section 4.1.1, the click-through result — Over the impression-matched window, parallel ads had a higher click-through rate.
quotes: At this early stage, parallel ads had a signiﬁcantly higher click-through rate

rows.value: (PDF p. 1) Abstract, the question — The paper's question is whether parallel feedback changes learning, self-efficacy and exploration.
quotes: Does creating and receiving feedback on multiple prototypes in parallel, as opposed to serially, affect learning, self-efﬁcacy, and design exploration?

rows.value: (PDF p. 6) Section 3.3.3, how the statements were written — The support here is a fixed vocabulary of design principles, chosen by a person from a closed list rather than generated, which makes this an experiment on the delivery schedule of a scaffold whose content is held constant.
quotes: Each category contained 12 to 20 statements intended to provide high-level direction without using explicitly positive or negative language.

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 3.5, session length — Everything here happens inside one sitting with an unfamiliar tool, so the self-efficacy change is a same-day shift and not a durable belief.
quotes: For 150 minutes of participation, subjects received $30 cash.

rows.value: medium · The design is strong and the manipulation is clean, but n is 33, the effects sit close to the threshold, and the two quality measures disagree with each other.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the clearest instance in the corpus so far of a semantic support measurably harming the person it was built to help, with the harm invisible in the artifact. The serial novices produced worse ads and also came out believing less in their own ability, and the authors offer a mechanism rather than an adjective for it: with one option there is nothing between the critique and the self. The design implication is not softer language, which was already neutral by construction, but giving a person something other than their only idea for the judgment to land on.

rows.value: Serial participants perceived the same expert feedback more negatively, and novices in the serial condition ended the session with lower confidence in their design ability than they started with, while novices in the parallel condition gained.
Earlier outline · Cognition and learning (now RQ2) · Earlier chapter · Conditional outcomes · S2Q3 · Limits and unanswered evidence

expert critique of a person's own creative work; novice designers; neutral, principle-stating critique attached to a single artifact; The statements were deliberately written without positive or negative language, and blind judges confirmed the experimenter chose comparably apt statements in both conditions, so the reaction is not explained by harsher content. (author stated); The harm concentrates in novices; participants with prior design experience did not show the reversal. (author stated)

The same critique statements were experienced as hostile by half the people who had only one design to attach them to, and by none of the people holding three.; receiving a critique; deciding whether to keep going; reading a critique as being about the work rather than about oneself
measured

empirically supported in paper · A pre- and post-task self-efficacy instrument, an analysis of variance with condition and prior experience as factors, and coded counts from open-ended exit interviews. · primary empirical

The nearest measure of anything lasting, what participants said they would do on a future project, went in the same direction but was not statistically significant. (author stated); Self-efficacy is self-reported on four Likert items about an hour and three quarters apart, inside the session that produced the reaction. Whether the loss survives the walk to the car is not observed. (reviewer inferred)
(PDF p. 17) Section 5, the critique read as an attack — Eight of seventeen serial participants called the feedback negative; no parallel participant did.
quotes: More notably, 8 of 17 of the serial participants reported the feedback as negative, compared to no such reports in the parallel condition

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) Section 4.4.4, the novice reversal — Novices gained 2.9 points of self-efficacy in parallel and lost 0.73 in serial.
quotes: novices reported a 2.9 increase in self-efﬁcacy in parallel, but a 0.73 decrease in serial

rows.value: (PDF p. 17) Section 5, the proposed reason — The proposed reason is that a single artifact leaves no distance between the person and the thing being judged.
quotes: With only one option there is no separation between designer and design. Parallel offers people distance between ego and object; serial conﬂates them.

rows.value: (PDF p. 15) Section 4.4.4, the summary of the novice effect — The self-efficacy effect is summarised as strongest for novices.
quotes: In short, parallel prototyping positively affected an individual’s belief in their ad design ability, especially for novices.

rows.value: (PDF p. 17) Section 5, the volunteering measure — Twelve of sixteen parallel participants volunteered their email against five of seventeen serial.
quotes: Twelve out of sixteen parallel participants provided their email, while only ﬁve of seventeen serial participants did the same

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 3.5, session length — Everything here happens inside one sitting with an unfamiliar tool, so the self-efficacy change is a same-day shift and not a durable belief.
quotes: For 150 minutes of participation, subjects received $30 cash.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: Worth carrying for the failure mode rather than the mechanism. A support that answers what should I change about this reliably produces a next version of this, and the participant quotes show people experiencing that as help. The paper's own null results mean the divergence-to-quality path should be recorded as untested here, not as demonstrated.

rows.value: Immediate feedback implicitly encourages refinement over exploration: serial participants produced measurably more similar prototypes and described using the feedback to decide where to go next, while parallel participants described making new ideas rather than copying their earlier ones.
Earlier outline · Work process (now RQ2) · Earlier chapter · Conditional outcomes · S2Q2 · Cumulative design knowledge · S2Q3 · Limits and unanswered evidence

open-ended design problems where many distinct solutions exist; individual designers under time pressure; critique arriving immediately after each attempt; The concern is specific to situated, incremental feedback, which the authors describe as steering toward a local optimum. (author stated)

People who got feedback after every attempt described following it and staying with one idea; people who got it in batches described starting over.; generating design alternatives; deciding what to do next; generating an alternative instead of refining the one at hand
measured

mixed or contested in paper · Fourteen thousand eight hundred and fifty crowd judgments of pairwise similarity across every participant's six prototypes, read alongside coded exit interviews. · primary empirical, author discussion

Divergence is offered as the reason parallel work came out better, but within this study similarity ratings did not predict either click performance or expert ratings. Both effects are real and they are not linked to each other by the data. (reviewer inferred); Experienced participants produced the least diverse sets and still outperformed novices, so diversity is not straightforwardly a virtue. (author stated)
(PDF p. 13) Section 4.2, the divergence result — Crowd raters judged parallel prototype sets more diverse than serial ones.
quotes: Serial ads were deemed signiﬁcantly more similar (μ = 3.25, SD = 1.96) than parallel ads (μ = 2.78, SD = 1.66) (F(1,14816) = 239.3, p < 0.05).

rows.value: (PDF p. 16) Section 5, a serial participant on following the feedback — A serial participant describes following the feedback and staying with one idea.
quotes: I would try to ﬁnd a good idea, and then use that idea and keep improving it and getting feedback. So I pretty much stuck with the same idea.

rows.value: (PDF p. 16) Section 5, the fixation reading — The measure and the interviews together are read as reduced fixation in parallel.
quotes: Both the divergence measure and the qualitative interviews suggest the parallel structure supports more generative thinking and reduces ﬁxation.

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Section 1, the problem iteration creates — The paper's premise is that situated feedback can steer a person to a local optimum.
quotes: Yet, its primary virtue— incremental, situated feedback—can also blind designers to other alternatives, steering them to local, rather than global, optima [Buxton 2007; Dow et al. 2009].

rows.value: (PDF p. 16) Section 5, delay as an advantage — The authors argue the delay built into parallel work is a benefit, not a cost.
quotes: On this view, the fact that parallel prototyping delays feedback is actually an advantage.

rows.value: (PDF p. 16) Section 5, why immediacy can hurt — Immediately available feedback is described as a crutch that blocks deeper understanding.
quotes: However, delay helps learners reﬂect: readily available, immediate feedback can be a crutch that discourages building a deep understanding

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) Section 4.2, the internal null on divergence — The proposed chain runs alternatives to divergence to better work, but divergence and quality were uncorrelated inside this study, so divergence is measured as a co-effect rather than shown to be the path.
quotes: Similarity ratings were not predictive (or inversely predictive) of online click performance

rows.value: medium · The divergence difference is measured on an enormous number of judgments and is not in doubt; what it explains is.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: The finding this review needs is the middle condition. A library of sound design principles, delivered to the wrong artifact, was worse on behaviour than silence. That separates two things a support can be praised for, being right and being aimed, and says only the second one bought anything here. It also puts a floor under the paper's main result: the parallel advantage is not a general effect of batching, it depends on the statements being chosen for the work.

(reviewer inferred)

items.lead: The portable idea is that the number of artifacts a support is attached to is part of the support's design, not a detail of the setting. Tohidi et al. established that alternatives free the critic; this paper closes the loop by showing they also protect the criticised. Any system that returns feedback on a single draft inherits the serial condition by default, which is a design decision most such systems make without noticing.

design education and studio critique; people whose work is being criticised; multiple concurrent alternatives authored by the same person; Built on Bandura's self-efficacy and on the finding that low self-efficacy makes a person read a critique of the work as a critique of themselves. (author stated)

cards.title: Towards a framework for investigating tangible environments for learning

rows.value: other
framework or design space, concept or theory, design principle

A framework paper with no results, proposing four parameters for the relation between a representation and the physical thing it belongs to: where it appears (on a separate screen, next to the object, or inside it), how the information reaches it (immediately and traceably, or accumulated and delayed; asked for, or triggered by accident), what it maps onto (an object that merely stands for the concept, or one that carries a property of it; a mapping that is direct, or one that is loose enough to argue about; and what the movement itself represents), and which sense carries it. The argument for organising a design space this way is that external representation is where the cognitive stakes are and that a decade of tangible-interface taxonomies had classified systems instead. Two things in it matter beyond tangibles. The paper states, as a design consequence rather than a finding, that making a phenomenon explicit may remove the computing that the learning consisted of, and that a concrete representation can bind understanding to one context and hide the abstraction it was meant to deliver. And it names the direct-against-ambiguous axis as pulling two ways at once: tight mappings let a person read the answer off, loose ones make them talk about it. Nothing here is tested; the authors say the framework's own value is still to be assessed.

medium · Read every claim on this card as a proposal. The paper has no participants, no measures and no results, and says so. Its value to this review is the vocabulary and two specific positions: that explicitness can cost the learner the work that was the learning, and that tightening a mapping trades reflection for offloading. Both are asserted here and evidenced elsewhere, and the citations are recorded so the evidence can be chased. The design space itself is untested and, by the authors' account, awaiting assessment.

sections.title: 7 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: Worth carrying for the cut it makes rather than for any evidence behind it. Most design spaces in this corpus describe what a support says; this one describes how a support is attached to the thing it is about. Where the representation appears relative to the artefact, whether the information arrives because you asked for it or because you happened to trigger it, how literally the object stands for the concept, and which sense carries it: none of those are properties of the content, and all of them are decisions someone makes. That framing survives the move out of tangibles, which is the reason to record it despite the paper having no results.

rows.value: A framework for tangible learning environments centred on external representation, with four parameters: location, the distance in space between the physical and digital components; dynamics, the flow of information including causality and intentionality; correspondence, the metaphorical mappings between object, representation, action and the learning concept; and modality, considered in parallel to the others.
Earlier outline · Design space (now RQ1) · Earlier chapter · Design space · S2Q2 · Cumulative design knowledge · S2Q1 · Concepts and lineage

tangible and embedded environments for learning; any support where a digital representation is coupled to a physical artefact and an action on it; learners, in the worked case children learning physical science; a digital representation coupled to an object and to the movement placed upon it; Offered as a structure for positioning research rather than a prescriptive comparison, and illustrated by a planned scenario rather than a result. (author stated); Three of the four parameters concern the relation between a representation and an artefact or an action, not the representation's content, so they carry to any support attached to a thing a person handles. (reviewer inferred)

Four things you can vary about a representation attached to a physical object: where it appears, how the information reaches it, what it maps onto, and which sense it arrives through.; designing a support that couples a physical artefact to digital information; planning a study of one; reading a representation against the thing it stands for
not measured · No study was run. Section 4 sets out three conditions that would vary location, and reports no data from them.

author proposed · Parameters derived from external cognition and embodied cognition theory, set against six prior tangible-interface taxonomies that are argued to classify systems without structuring an investigation of cognitive effect. · framework derivation, theoretical argument

The framework's own value is stated as still to be assessed. Nothing in the paper tests any parameter. (author stated); The authors decline to make it comparative, on the grounds that comparison would demand consistency of metaphor across interfaces that do not share one. (author stated)
(PDF p. 9) Section 3, the four parameters — The framework is four parameters: where the representation sits, how information flows to it, what it maps onto, and in which sense modality.
quotes: The location parameter refers to the distance in space between physical and digital components of the system; dynamics is related to the flow of information throughout the interaction, including links between action, intention, and feedback; and correspondence depicts the metaphors involved in the nature of representations of artefacts and actions upon them. The modality of representation impacts on different aspects of the whole interaction and is therefore considered in parallel to all other categories (see fig. 1).

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 3, what the framework does — The organising relation is representation against artefact against action.
quotes: Our framework builds on concepts from previous frameworks and seeks to address some of the issues raised by focusing the external representation-action-artefact relationships that occur in tangible environments as a way of conceptualising physical-digital links and analysing their effects from a learning perspective.

rows.value: (PDF p. 2) Abstract, the contribution — The stated contribution is a structure for investigating differential cognitive effect.
quotes: Taking external representation as the central focus, this paper proposes a framework for investigating the effect of tangible technologies on interaction and cognition. Key artefact-action-representation relationships are identified, and classified to form a structure for investigating the differential cognitive effect of these features.

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 3, the object itself as representation — The object itself is treated as a representation, not only as a carrier of one.
quotes: A focus on representation offers the means to better understand the role of tangibles for learning, not only in terms of representation linked to artefacts but also in terms of the manipulative as representation, rather than as an object in itself.

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Section 1, the combinatorial problem — The motivation is that flexible coupling produces an unmanageable number of research factors.
quotes: The potential to exploit different forms of digital representations and flexibly link them with physical artefacts and action promises greater representational power. However, such flexibility of couplings brings with it an exponential number of factors for research.

rows.value: (PDF p. 9) Section 3, the four parameters — Three of the four parameters are about the relation between a representation and something else rather than about the representation's content, which is a different cut from most design spaces in this corpus and transfers past tangibles.
quotes: The location parameter refers to the distance in space between physical and digital components of the system; dynamics is related to the flow of information throughout the interaction, including links between action, intention, and feedback; and correspondence depicts the metaphors involved in the nature of representations of artefacts and actions upon them. The modality of representation impacts on different aspects of the whole interaction and is therefore considered in parallel to all other categories (see fig. 1).

rows.value: (PDF p. 17) Section 5, nothing is tested yet — Nothing in this paper is tested. Every parameter is a proposal, and the empirical warrant is entirely carried in from cited studies of other systems.
quotes: As part of the current research, the value of this framework will be assessed and iteratively refined.

rows.value: medium · A well-argued and clearly sourced framework with no empirical support of its own. The parameters are defensible as a vocabulary; whether they carve the space at the joints is untested here and by the authors' own account still to be assessed.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the review's central tension stated in one sentence, in 2008, as something a designer has to decide rather than something a study found. A support that shows a person what is happening spares them the computing; where the computing was the learning, the sparing is the loss. The paper adds the second half that is easy to miss: a concrete representation does not automatically deliver the abstraction it stands for, and can prevent it. Both halves arrive as citations rather than as results, so the value here is the framing, and the sources are where the evidence would be chased.

rows.value: Explicit depiction of phenomena through external representations, physical and digital, may reduce cognitive computation and the active working out that is instrumental for learning; and concrete representations carry the further risk of narrowing comprehension to a specific context and blinding students to the general nature of the abstract concept.
Earlier outline · Cognition and learning (now RQ2) · Earlier chapter · Conditional outcomes · Earlier chapter · Definition and lineage · S2Q3 · Limits and unanswered evidence

learning, as distinct from performing; learners for whom the working out is the point; an external representation that depicts the phenomenon explicitly; The benefit side is established: an explicit depiction eases problem solving, supports inference and frees attention for the task. (author stated); The cost side is stated for concrete representations specifically: the link to the abstract concept is not always transparent, and concreteness can bind understanding to one context. (author stated)

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The most usable claim in the paper, because it names a dial and says which way each end of it points. Every support in this corpus that labels, summarises or depicts sits somewhere on this dial, and the usual assumption is that tighter is better. The counter-position here is that looseness is what produces talk, and that talk is where meaning gets settled between people. It is a proposal built on two studies of other systems, and the paper is scrupulous about not claiming more.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Recorded because the same variable exists wherever a support is shown alongside the work it is about, and is almost never treated as a variable. A suggestion in a side panel, in a tooltip on the thing itself, or rendered into the artifact are the same three values under different names, and this paper says the choice among them decides how much attention the link costs and what the person can still do with their hands. items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The distinction between an effect a person asked for and one that arrived anyway is the timing question this review meets repeatedly under other names: pulled against pushed, on request against always on. What this paper adds is the second axis crossing it, whether the person can tell which of their actions caused the effect. A support whose response accumulates over several actions and then arrives late is not simply slower; it breaks the link between doing and seeing, and the paper is honest that nobody has measured what that costs.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.small: contradiction, concept or lineage, open question
items.lead: Two things here are worth the corpus's attention. The first is the diagnosis, which this review keeps rediscovering in other subfields twenty years later: engagement is easy to measure and gets measured, learning is hard to measure and gets asserted. The second is the specific move the paper makes against Fishkin, that a taxonomy dimension can smuggle a causal assumption into what looks like a descriptive scheme, in this case that familiar direct mapping is the more powerful. That is a methodological warning about design spaces in general, including the one this paper then builds.

rows.value: Studies of tangible learning systems primarily report engagement, enjoyment and technical achievement; concrete findings about learning gains are minimal and the role of representational relationships is rarely explicit. The existing frameworks are descriptive taxonomies of systems and none structures a systematic investigation of cognitive effect; one of them, in defining tangibility by metaphor, assumes without evidence that direct mapping to familiar physical tools is more powerful.

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) Section 2.2, taxonomies describe rather than structure — They classify to describe and compare, without defining what representations do for learning.

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) Section 2.2, Fishkin's two dimensions — Fishkin's two dimensions are embodiment and metaphor.
quotes: Fishkin (2004) provides a taxonomy to locate, compare and integrate research in tangible interfaces defining them in terms of levels of tangibility using two dimensions each with four levels: embodiment specifies the relative distance between the physical and digital display; metaphor specifies how close the effect of user action is to the real world effect of similar actions.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The weakest of the four parameters and still worth recording, because the transience point generalises. cards.title: Evaluating user interface systems research
cards.meta: 2007 · Proceedings of the 20th Annual ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology · doi 10.1145/1294211.1294256 · Route C

rows.value: other
concept or theory, lineage or history, framework or design space, design principle, failure or counterevidence, measurement or method

The paper does not invoke a formal scaffolding or learning theory. It derives a conceptual evaluation framework from UI-systems practice and uses Semantic Pointing, Menulay, and GIGO as precedents illustrating model mismatch, lowered skill barriers, and changing sources of expressive leverage; these precedents are conceptually used but not operationalized as a tested theory.

medium · The paper provides clear, transferable constructs, mechanisms, failure modes, and evaluation criteria, but it is a conceptual methodological argument supported by examples rather than an empirical test of artifact, process, learning, or transfer outcomes.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-03

cards.title: Scaffolding self-regulated learning and metacognition - implications for the design of computer-based scaffolds

rows.value: S2W-30FD6C9070DFCF9DFC546952
other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle

An editorial introduction, not a study, and worth reading as the field's own statement of what it thought scaffolding meant once it moved onto computers. It gives a four-part decomposition, diagnosis, calibrated support, fading and individualization, and that is its durable contribution: it turns scaffolding from a metaphor into a set of attributes an artifact either has or lacks. Fixed against adaptive is then defined by two of the four, who diagnoses and whether support is calibrated to a person, with fading admitted only as something adaptive scaffolding may include. A second distinction runs by source, from the learner's own questioning, through static prompts and templates in the environment, to an external human or artificial agent. The article carries no data. Every result in it is a one-sentence report of one of the five companion papers, the headline one being the lead author's own: adaptive scaffolding moved students toward more sophisticated mental models, raised declarative knowledge and raised the frequency of some self-regulated learning strategies. No sample size, statistic or effect size appears anywhere in thirteen pages, and Table 1 is six rows by five columns of phrases without a single number. Nothing is measured after support is withdrawn. The authors themselves say effectiveness is hard to establish because these environments bundle several supports and several agents at once, and then report the findings without returning to that problem.

high · What the article says is clear; what it establishes is almost nothing. It is an editorial introduction of ten body pages with no data, no participants and no statistics anywhere, and Table 1 is six rows by five columns of phrases without a single number. The framework part is firm because it is stated plainly and used consistently: four attributes, a fixed-adaptive range defined by diagnosis and individualization, a source continuum, and a score of three of five studies as lacking calibration or fading. Everything empirical is a one-sentence report of a companion paper, and the headline one is the lead author's own study in the issue he edited. The authors themselves say effectiveness cannot be attributed in environments that bundle several supports and agents, and then report findings without returning to that. Nothing is measured after support is withdrawn. The printing is careless in ways that bear on the summaries: a missing noun, six questions announced as five, and the first author's name misspelled in his own table header on three pages.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The one thing here that a design review can carry forward. Scaffolding stops being a metaphor and becomes four attributes an artifact either has or lacks: diagnosis, calibrated support, fading, individualization. Because the definition admits human tutors, computer tutors, teachers and animated agents as sources, the four attributes apply to a person and to a worksheet on the same terms, which is what lets the article score a paper metanavigational scaffold and a live human tutor in one table. Two further kind-distinctions are offered and neither is developed: scaffolds are named conceptual, metacognitive, procedural and strategic in one italicised phrase with a string of citations behind it; and the target of support may be domain knowledge, one's own learning, use of the environment itself, or adapting to an instructional context, with declarative, procedural, conceptual or metacognitive knowledge inside each. The four attributes are the part that does work, because Table 1 uses them as a scoring sheet and three of the five studies score negative on calibration, individualization or fading. None of this is tested. It is a definition, offered in the first three pages, and the rest of the article applies it.

rows.value: Scaffolding involves providing assistance to students on an as-needed basis, fading the assistance as learner competence increases (Wood et al., 1976). Scaffolds are tools, strategies, and guides used by human and computer tutors, teachers, and animated pedagogical agents during learning to enable them to develop understandings beyond their immediate grasp. [...] Scaffolding involves calibrated support for diagnosed learning targets. Four attributes associated with scaffolding include: diagnosis, calibrated support, fading, and individualization.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: This is the fixed against adaptive cut, and it is worth being exact about where the article puts it. Adaptive means ongoing diagnosis and calibration to the individual learner; fading enters only as something adaptive scaffolding 'may include'. At the other end sits student self-diagnosis with no individualized support and no fading. So the axis is who diagnoses and whether support is pitched at a person, not whether the support is delivered by machine or human and not whether it fades. Table 1 is the cut applied: three of the five studies are marked as having no calibrated support, no individualized support or no fading support, and the running text confirms that Dabbagh and Kitsantas, Choi and Puntambekar and Stylianou neither calibrated to the individual nor used a human agent to diagnose. The only place a fixed condition is described concretely is a table cell: fixed scaffolding is guided questions calibrated to the study session rather than to the student. One sentence carries a lineage claim the article never develops, that diagnosis is what separates the original conception of scaffolding from later uses of the word; it is asserted in nine words and dropped.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A second axis, cutting across the first: who or what supplies the support. Three positions are named, the learner's own questioning, static prompts or templates inside the environment, and an external human or artificial agent. The five studies are then placed along it, and the placements are concrete enough to be useful: a paper-based metanavigational scaffold and embedded static scaffolds at one end; web-based pedagogical tools with a distance instructor giving individualized feedback on a proposal in the middle; fixed scaffolds in the environment set against dynamic adaptive tutoring by a human regulating agent, and less formal human scaffolding across a year-long course project, at the other. What the article does not do is separate this axis from the first one. Its headline comparison varies adaptivity and the agent together, machine-fixed against human-adaptive, so the continuum runs diagonally and no cell of the article isolates an adaptive machine or a fixed human. The design implications the paper closes with, that pedagogical agents should diagnose, calibrate and fade, are precisely a request for the cell it never occupies.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This is where the review's own question about withdrawal lands, and the answer is a clean no. Fading is one of the four attributes named on page 370, and Table 1 records it study by study: temporary fading for Azevedo, fading for Hadwin, no fading support for Puntambekar and Stylianou, gradually remove limits and control from other to student for Dabbagh and Kitsantas. Yet no outcome in the article is measured after support was taken away. The single place withdrawal is observed rather than asserted is the Hadwin study, and what it measured is the shape of the talk while the year ran: a significant fall in dialogue about defining the task, and rises in dialogue about enacting strategies and setting goals, as the instructor pulled back and students spoke more. That is a redistribution of who regulates what, recorded during an ongoing project, and the article reports it without any accompanying measure of the students' work or of what they could do afterwards with no instructor present. Fading then reappears in the closing list as a thing pedagogical agents ought to do, which returns the article's own definition to the status of future work.

cards.title: Mapping training: the transfer of a cognitive technology for improving counseling

rows.value: other
failure or counterevidence, design principle, primary empirical

A retrospective account by the group that built node-link mapping for drug abuse counselling, written to explain why a technique with a decade of positive trials behind it did not stay in use. The central observation is the one this review most needs: once the studies ended and the pressure of the research protocol was gone, many counsellors across all the research sites reduced or stopped their mapping. Some said they had internalised the principles and no longer needed to map overtly; others, in the authors' words, seemed just relieved to stop, and the paper has no way to tell those two apart. It also names a cause that implicates the trial design itself: counsellors were given no choice about being trained, because that choice was the difference between treatment groups, and interviews suggested the resulting regimentation reduced their enthusiasm once the experimental phase was over. The middle of the paper is an unusually candid record of a structure-versus-ownership trade. Free mapping overloaded counsellors in one-to-one sessions, so pre-formed fill-in-the-blank guide maps were introduced; those cut the overload and produced a lack of personal ownership and a reduction in spontaneity, and use recovered only when counsellors drew their own. Two later workshops give the only numbers: after a four-hour session that scored the highest relevance rating of four workshops, 24 per cent of 25 respondents had used mapping six weeks later; after a redesigned session built around practice, choice, peer tables and an explicit implementation plan, 87 per cent of 16 respondents had at three months. The authors say plainly that the follow-up intervals differ and that what was reported is probably exploration rather than routine practice.

medium · The observations are rare and the evidence behind them is thin, and the authors say so. The decay after the protocol ended, the regimentation explanation and the guide-map trade are all reported from informal observation and counsellor comments over the life of a project, with the authors stating that they will in future develop a formal system for gathering this kind of data; there are no counts, no before-and-after rates, no denominators and no tests for any of it. The two workshop follow-ups are the only numbers in the paper and they are self-reported use from 25 and 16 respondents at 54 and 53 per cent response rates, at 1.5 and 3 months, in two different regions with no control and no random assignment. The authors flag the interval difference themselves and add that the reported use most likely reflects exploration rather than routine practice. Treat the decay observation and the ownership trade as well-motivated field testimony from the people who built the tool, worth more than their statistical support because almost nobody else reports this stage at all, and treat the 24 versus 87 per cent contrast as a hypothesis, not a result.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The stage this review keeps failing to find, reported by the people who built the tool. The support in question is not the map itself but the apparatus around it - training, workshops, personal coaching, phone feedback, and a protocol that obliged counsellors to send their maps to the researchers - and when that apparatus was withdrawn the practice largely stopped, across every site, despite a decade of positive patient outcomes behind it. Two things make it worth carrying beyond drug treatment. First, the two possible readings of the drop are given side by side and cannot be separated: some counsellors said they had internalised the principles and no longer needed to map overtly, which is exactly what successful fading looks like, and others were simply relieved to stop, which is what dependence and resentment look like. Reduced use of a support is the same observable in both cases, so use counts alone cannot measure fading; only the work itself, measured after the support is gone, can. Nobody measured the counselling. Second, what survived was specific: pre-formed guide maps kept being used for fixed activities like treatment planning, while flexible mapping faded to occasional. This is field testimony, not data - no rates, no denominators, no tests.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The conditions that made the efficacy trial valid are named as a cause of the practice not surviving it. Assigning counsellors to mapping without choice was not an oversight - it was what made a treatment group a treatment group - and the authors report that the resulting sense of one more mandated procedure left counsellors unenthusiastic once the requirement lifted. This is a standing conflict worth carrying into any synthesis of supports. Demonstrating that a support works usually requires imposing it uniformly; producing people who go on using it appears to require the opposite. It follows that durability observed inside or just after a trial is not a clean estimate of the support's durability in the wild, because the trial has manufactured part of the resistance it then measures, and that the literature on whether supports last is systematically contaminated by how it is produced. The paper's own remedy runs the same way: freedom to choose one's own strategies with a trainer's encouragement is what it says is key to lasting use. All of this rests on counsellor interviews reported without counts.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A complete cycle of the structure trade, observed in a working setting over several years. Free mapping asked counsellors to invent the representation while running a session and overloaded them, so most stopped and the maps they did produce were cryptic. Pre-formed fill-in-the-blank maps removed the overload and introduced two new costs the authors name precisely: a lack of personal ownership and a reduction in spontaneity, with the structure simultaneously lowering cognitive load and raising restrictiveness and the sense of external control. The resolution is the part worth carrying, because it is not a point on the line between too much structure and too little: use recovered when counsellors authored their own guide maps, with staff drafting from interviews for those who would not draw. The variable that moved behaviour was authorship, not amount. The same paper states both failure modes explicitly - some counsellors found free mapping too much cognitive effort, others found guide maps inflexible and alien - and adds a bootstrapping problem it calls an irony: the tool is hard to use until you have enough experience to see where it applies, so unguided exploration frustrated some while broad encouragement produced inappropriate use. All of it is observational, with no counts anywhere.

These problems were addressed by encouraging counselors to create their own guide maps, tailored to their own approaches and needs... items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Immediate satisfaction and later use came apart in the same sample. The workshop scored the highest relevance rating of the four presented, at 4.1 on a five-point scale, and its participants stated their intention to use the material; six weeks later fewer than a quarter of the respondents had. The paper makes the same point twice more: manuals were downloaded and purchased substantially with little indication of actual use, and conference workshops drew high ratings and almost no follow-up contact. For a review of supports this is a measurement lesson rather than a finding about counselling. Exit ratings, stated intentions and download counts are all measures of the moment of exposure, and this paper shows all three failing to predict the behaviour they are usually taken to stand for. It also matters for reading the wider literature: an evaluation that stopped at the questionnaire would have recorded this workshop as a success. The bounds are real - 25 respondents at a 54 per cent response rate, self-reported use, one interval, no control - so treat the dissociation as demonstrated in this case and the percentage as indicative.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The paper's one attempt to design for durability, and the four changes are worth recording even though the evidence for them is weak. Presentation time was cut in favour of hands-on practice with the trainer moved from sage on the stage to guide on the side; the system was broken into independent tools presented as a buffet the participant chooses from; peers were seated in tables of five or six to coach each other through practice and role play; and half an hour was set aside for each person to complete a planning map naming a date, time and context for a first attempt, with fall-back contingencies. Every one of those addresses a cause the earlier half of the paper identified - overload, lack of ownership, dependence on the trainer, and the gap between intention and action - which is more design coherence than most training studies offer. What cannot be concluded is that they worked. Two regions, no randomisation, no control, 16 and 25 respondents at about half response, self-reported use, and follow-up at 3 months against 1.5. The authors say the interval difference may partly explain the gain, and that what was reported is probably exploration rather than routine practice. Four changes made together cannot be separated.

cards.title: Analyzing human–computer interaction as distributed cognition: The resources model

rows.value: S2W-C2BC1C535DC36FA581F31E3E
other
concept or theory, framework or design space, design principle, lineage or history

The founding attempt to turn distributed cognition into something an interface analyst can use. Wright, Fields and Harrison argue that distributed cognition makes external resources for action central but never defines them well enough to analyse anything, so they supply the definition: six abstract information structures a support can carry, which are plans, goals, possibilities, history, action-effect relations and states, each able to sit in the head, in the artifact, or be split; and four ways of deciding what to do next, each with a stated list of which structures it requires. Three things are worth carrying. That strategy-to-resource table is a design space in one page, saying which ways of working a configuration of support permits and which it forecloses. The co-location principle is concrete and reusable: coordination gets cheap when the resources a strategy must bring together sit in the same external space, which is why a speed bug beside the airspeed needle turns arithmetic into looking. And the Chart Wizard analysis names a failure mode in the authors' own words: a plan externalised one dialogue box at a time drives the interaction rather than resourcing it, confounding control structure with information resource, so the user can neither see the plan nor work another way. What the paper does not contain is evidence. The authors say outright that they do not aim to validate the model empirically and that the right validation is uptake by designers. Their one study, an 8 puzzle from an unpublished MSc thesis, is reported with no sample size, measure or statistic. And across 82,477 folded characters the words scaffolding, fading, withdrawal, contingency, dependence and over-reliance appear zero times.

high · High as a source of vocabulary and design distinctions, near zero as a source of evidence, and the paper says so itself. It is a 37-page theory article in a top journal, and its conceptual work is careful: the six structures and four strategies are defined, the abstract-versus-representation distinction is held consistently, and a cockpit checklist, a spreadsheet wizard and a sliding tile puzzle are each worked through in detail. But the authors state in the introduction that they do not aim to validate the model by testing its predictions, and in the conclusion that validation means uptake by designers. Every empirical statement is either a summary of someone else's study or a forward reference to work reported elsewhere. The one study claimed as their own, the 8 puzzle variations, is an unpublished MSc thesis by a student of the first author, reported with no sample size, task measure, move count or test; the sentence claiming stronger evidence than a prior published study has nothing printed behind it. The Chart Wizard walkthrough is one analyst's prediction about one hypothetical user, never tested. Read it for what it defines; treat every claim about people as untested.

sections.title: 6 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: This is a design space for external support stated as a vocabulary plus a requirements table, and it is the most directly reusable thing in the paper. Six structures name what a support can carry: the plan, the goal, the set of currently possible actions, the history of what has been done, the mapping from action to effect, and the current state. Each may sit in the person's head, in the artifact, or be split between them. Four strategies name ways of working, and Figure 2 says which structures each one requires, so a configuration of support can be read off against which ways of working it enables and which it forecloses. Withhold history and history-based choice becomes unavailable; withhold action-effect information and both goal matching and plan construction lose an input they need. That turns a vague question about how much help to give into a specific question about which structures a design externalises, and it applies to any support for structured work rather than only to graphical interfaces. What it does not do is order the configurations. The model says which strategies a configuration permits, never which configuration is better, and it has no vocabulary for a configuration that should change over time.

(PDF p. 15) 2.1 Abstract Information Structures — The core definition: six abstract information structures, which are plans, goals, possibilities, history, action-effect relations and states, derived inductively from the HCI and CSCW literature, found sufficient for the analyses done so far, and explicitly open to extension.
quotes: The resources model identifies six information structures that can be de- fined at an abstract level in the same way that Zhang (1996) defined the RIDs taxonomy and Zhang and Norman (1994) defined the information structures of the Tower of Hanoi. That is, the type and structure of the information can be described independently of how it may be represented in an information arti- fact. In this section we first describe the abstract information structures that constitute the building blocks of the resources model. Second, we give exam- ples of the different ways these abstract information structures can be repre- sented for use as resources. The abstract information structures are as follows:  Plans.  Goals.  Possibilities.  History.  Actioneffect relations.  States. These types have been derived from the HCI and CSCW literature in an in- ductive way. We have found these six basic structures sufficient for the kinds of analyses we have so far carried out and believe they form a coherent core for HCI modeling. However, it is entirely possible that more structures could be required

rows.value: (PDF p. 20) 2.2 Interaction Strategies — The reciprocal relation at the centre of the framework: a strategy presupposes a configuration of resources to be effective, and a configuration makes particular strategies possible; the list of strategies is declared sufficient rather than exhaustive.
quotes: Interaction strategies presuppose certain configurations of resources to make them effective and, conversely, a particular configuration of resources makes particular interaction strategies possible. In the following, we de- scribe a range of interaction strategies relevant to HCI and relate these to the information resources they require. Like our abstract information structures, we do not suppose that this is an exhaustive list. Rather, it is sufficient for our purposes
