rows.value: (PDF p. 15) 2.1 Abstract Information Structures, Plans — How one structure is defined and how structures interlock: a plan is a sequence of actions, events or states that could be carried out, and using one requires knowing where you are in it, which is done by combining the plan with a representation of history.
quotes: The idea of a plan as a resource for action comes from the work of Suchman (1987) and Schmidt (1997). In the resources model, a plan is a sequence of actions, events, or states that could be carried out. Plans can in- volve conditional branches and loops that are dependent on the state of the system (see next). When using a plan, it is important to know where one is in the plan. This can be achieved, for example, by combining the plan with a representation of the history of actions so far carried out

rows.value: (PDF p. 17) 2.1 Representing Abstract Information Structures, Plans — The abstract-to-representation move: the same plan can be memorised, printed as a standard operating procedure, or split, and position within it can be held by a thumb or finger beside the last action or by ticking items off.
quotes: sented externally in the interface; internally in the head of the user; or, more often, distributed across the two. Plans. Plans can be represented internally as memorized procedures to complete some task. They can also be represented externally as standard operating procedures, or step-by-step instructions for achieving some goal. If a person is following a plan, it is important to know exactly where in the plan he or she is. The sequence of actions constituting the plan can be externalized in a written procedure, in which case, ones current position may be represented by a thumb or finger placed alongside the last action or perhaps by ticking off those actions already done

rows.value: (PDF p. 19) 2.2 Cyclic Models of Interaction — The process half of the model: action is informed by whatever configuration of resources is represented at that moment, internally or externally, taking an action changes the configuration, at minimum by changing the history, and the new configuration informs the next action.
quotes: The resources model is also a cyclic model, but the distinction between user and environment and between information and control flow is deemphasized. Plans as control structures, for example, can be external or internal to the user or distributed between user and system. The model is cyclic in the sense that action is informed by the configuration of resources represented in the interaction at any particular time, either externally in the interface or internally in the head of the user. When an action is taken, the configuration of resources is changed. Minimally, for example, the history of the interaction always changes when an action is taken. This new configuration of resources is then used to consider the next action

rows.value: (PDF p. 3) Abstract — The two-part structure of the contribution: abstract information structures plus interaction strategies, which through coordination and integration supply a link among devices, representations and actions that the distributed cognition literature does not articulate.
quotes: The resources model uses the concept of interaction strategy to describe the way in which different configurations of resources can differently shape users actions. These 2 components of the resources model (information structures and interaction strategies), through the process of coordination and integration, provide a link among devices, representations, and actions that is not well articulated in the DC literature

rows.value: medium · The definitions are clear, internally consistent and applied without slippage across three very different examples, which is real evidence that the vocabulary can be used. That it is the right or a complete vocabulary is asserted, and the paper offers no way to test it.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A lineage claim with a named defect, which makes it useful to a review that has to explain where the language of external support came from. The paper pulls together three streams that had not been read as one: Hutchins's field studies of cockpits and warships, where the unit of analysis is a network of people and artifacts; Zhang and Norman's laboratory work on the Tower of Hanoi, where the same problem is made easier or harder purely by moving rules between the apparatus and memory; and the display-based interaction models of the late 1980s, which found that experts could not recall menu names yet used menus fluently. The common finding is that competence is a property of the person-plus-artifact pairing rather than of the person. The defect the authors name is that none of these accounts says how a representation turns into an action; representational analyses treat a task as something a display supports more or less well, and stop there. The resolution they adopt from Suchman is that a plan is a resource for action rather than a control structure that is executed, which is the pivot that lets an external artifact hold a plan without deciding what the person does. That distinction is exactly what the paper's own failure case later turns on.

rows.value: DC research identifies resources for action as central to the interaction between people and technologies, but it stops short of providing a definition of such resources at a level that could be used to analyze interaction... However, as it stands, the DC paradigm has some limitations as an approach to analyzing HCI. Central to such a model there needs to be an account of action.

quotes: DC research identifies resources for action as central to the interaction be- tween people and technologies, but it stops short of providing a definition of such resources at a level that could be used to analyze interaction. The re- sources model described in this article defines a limited number of resource types as abstract information structures that can be used to analyze interac- tion

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) 1.2 Motivation for the Resources Model — The diagnosis of what distributed cognition lacks: an account of action. Goal-based models tie representation to action through operators or an execution-evaluation loop, whereas the representational analyses treat tasks as something a representation supports more or less well.
quotes: However, as it stands, the DC paradigm has some limitations as an ap- proach to analyzing HCI. Central to such a model there needs to be an ac- count of action. We see this in all HCI models. For example, the GOMS concept of operations ties goal representations to action (Card et al., 1983), and in a less formal account, Normans (1988) executionevaluation loop links the mental representation of plans to actions and their effects on the world. In contrast, Zhangs (1996) RIDs framework is concerned more with inferences drawn from representations, and tasks are seen as something supported more or less by representations

rows.value: (PDF p. 13) 1.2 Motivation for the Resources Model — The contested inheritance about plans: in artificial intelligence and in GOMS a plan is an internal control structure that is deterministically followed, whereas for Hutchins and more forcefully for Suchman a plan is a resource for action, which requires plans to be objects of attention that can be manipulated and externalised.
quotes: But, in artificial intelligence, as with the GOMS style of modeling, a plan is seen as a control structure or program that is internal and usually deterministically fol- lowed. The alternative view put forward by Hutchins (1995a) and more force- fully by Suchman (1987) is that plans are resources for action rather than program-like control structures. To make sense of plans as resources for ac- tion, plans themselves must be seen as possible objects of conscious attention

rows.value: (PDF p. 5) 1.1 Distributed Cognition — The two traditions being merged: cognitive anthropology, which studies artifacts in real work settings through field study, and cognitive psychology, which studies the individual in a technological environment and centres the distinction between knowledge in the head and in the world.
quotes: Cognitive science research on the distributed nature of cognition comes from two distinct but not independent intellectual traditions: cognitive anthro- pology and cognitive psychology. In the former, the emphasis is on the study of real-world settings and the role that artifacts play in the practice of work. The research is based on field studies and relates most naturally to the con- cerns of CSCW. The emphasis of the latter is the study of the individual in a technological environment, and the distinction between knowledge in the head and in the world is central. Although everyday work is taken seriously, there is a laboratory tradition at the heart of this approach. Both of these tradi- tions are reviewed in this section, and the commonalities between them drawn out as a motivation for the resources model

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) 1.1 The Anthropology of Hutchins — The Hutchins position summarised: the unit of analysis is a network of technologies and actors, and cognition is the coordination of distributed internal and external representations into a robust information-processing system.
quotes: As these examples show, a key feature of DC theory in the Hutchins tradi- tion is that the unit of analysis is a network of technologies and actors. Cogni- tion is viewed as a process of coordinating distributed internal and external representations to provide a robust information-processing system. Whereas Hutchinss emphasis was on team work, others from cognitive psychology took a DC approach to individual problem solving, where the emphasis has been on how cognitive components of a problem are distributed between a single human problem solver and a single problem-solving artifact

rows.value: (PDF p. 7) 1.1 Distributed Cognition in Psychology — The Norman position summarised: information embedded in artifacts matters as much as knowledge in the head, well-designed artifacts reduce what users must remember and badly designed ones increase the knowledge demand, and the rhetorical point of the distinction was to show designers that design decisions have cognitive consequences.
quotes: Norman (1988) popularized the idea that knowledge may be as much in the world as it is in the head. Normans aim here was to point out that the informa- tion embedded in technological artifacts was as important to the achievement of a task as the knowledge residing in the mind of the individual who used that artifact. Furthermore, Norman (1988) argued that well-designed artifacts could reduce the need for users to remember large amounts of information, whereas badly designed artifacts increased the knowledge demands made on the user. items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The most portable design rule in the paper, and the one that costs nothing to apply. What a support costs its user is not settled by which information it holds but by where that information sits relative to everything else the person must hold at the same moment. Two worked examples make it concrete. On an airspeed indicator with a speed bug, the target and the current value occupy one dial, so comparing them is a glance; put the target in memory and the same comparison becomes reading a numeral, recalling a number and doing arithmetic. On a paper checklist, a finger laid beside the last completed item fuses the plan and the history into a single representation, and the second example is the more instructive because the user manufactures the co-location that the artifact failed to provide. The general form is that the expensive part of using a support is bringing its pieces together, so a design should be assessed on which pairs of resources a strategy forces the person to hold at once and how far apart those pairs are. The paper offers no way to quantify any of this. Coordination cost is argued from examples, never measured, and there is no scale on which two designs could be compared.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: A failure mode named precisely, in a vocabulary that makes it diagnosable rather than merely deplorable. A step-by-step wizard holds the entire plan and shows one step at a time. That is enough for the user to finish the task and not enough for them to see what the task is, so the plan cannot be internalised, and because the same artifact both holds the information and enforces the order, no other way of working is left open. The authors' phrase for it is that control structure and information resource are confounded, and the distinction it rests on is the one they took from Suchman at the start: a plan can be a resource you consult or a program that runs you, and a support that fuses the two removes the person's ability to depart from it. This is directly transferable to any modern step-through assistant, and it is worth noting that the same paper shows the well-designed opposite in the printed checklist, where the whole plan is visible at once and the user marks their own position. Two qualifications matter. The wizard is not simply worse: the paper's comparison shows it externalising a plan that the unconstrained dialogue box leaves the user to remember, and the analysis credits it with characteristics that enhance usability. And the whole thing is one analyst's walkthrough of one hypothetical user. The difficulty of internalising is a may, the errors at step two are a prediction, and nobody was observed.

rows.value: Externalizing the plan resource as a sequence of dialogue boxes may make it difficult for the user to internalize the plan (at least in any direct way) because it is implicit. In addition, it does not support the development of alternative interaction strategies because the plan as externalized does not resource the interaction. Rather, it drives it in the sense of enforcing a plan-following strategy. That is, control structure and information resource are confounded in this particular design solution. Such confounding limits users in terms of what they can do and how they can develop and adapt their strategies.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The paper's one empirical claim, and it is reported so thinly that it cannot be used as evidence for anything. The design idea behind it is good: take one task, vary only which resources are externalised and how, and see whether the way people go about the task changes. The variants are described clearly enough to reconstruct, including a goal shown as a separate display, a goal printed as a background map behind the tiles, a goal signalled only by feedback when a tile is correctly placed, and a colour version built specifically to block the internal route because an arbitrary colour arrangement is hard to memorise while a numeric sequence is not. That last variant is the sharpest instrument here, since it isolates the external resource by removing the internal substitute, and it is the manoeuvre a study of any support would need in order to attribute an effect to the support rather than to what the person already knows. But no result is reported. There is no sample size, no task measure, no move count, no comparison and no statistical test, only the assertion that the studies showed the externalisations affect strategy. The work is an unpublished MSc thesis by a student of the first author, cited three times, and the sentence claiming stronger evidence than a published study has nothing printed behind it. Carry the design, not the conclusion.

rows.value: Golightly and Gilmore (1997) argued that the directness of manipulation was the significant factor in determining a users method. Our studies, by using versions that differed only in the resource representations, provide stronger evidence that the design of external resources is an important factor in determining interaction strategy. These are, however, only laboratory studies of a simple puzzle.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: Two absences sit on top of each other here, and together they characterise a whole lineage. The first is declared: the authors twice state that they are not validating the model against outcomes and that the right test is adoption by designers. That is a coherent position for a vocabulary paper, and it means nothing in this article can be cited as evidence about what happens to a person. The second absence is demonstrable rather than declared. Folding the whole extracted text to lowercase alphanumerics, the substrings scaffold, fading, fade, withdraw, contingen, vygotsk, dependence and overreliance each occur zero times across 82,477 characters, while externaliz occurs 33 times and expert occurs 10. So the founding attempt to define what an external support can hold produced a rich vocabulary for the contents of a support and none whatever for changing or removing those contents as the person changes. The model describes a configuration and how it changes when an action is taken; it has no term for a configuration that should be different next week because the user is different. The nearest thing to a learning concern in the whole article is one hedged sentence about a wizard being hard to internalise, and the only expertise discussion is a static contrast between what novices and experts already know. This matters for a review of supports because the vocabulary that shaped how human-computer interaction talks about external resources for the following two decades had no place in it for withdrawal, and the gap starts here rather than being introduced later.

cards.title: Variatio est mater studiorum
cards.meta: 2000 · Higher education research \& development · doi 10.1080/07294360020021455 · Route C

rows.value: other
concept or theory, design principle, framework or design space

A fourteen-page theoretical address arguing that you can only learn to see what you have seen vary: no discernment without variation, and therefore no learning without it. Three things are worth carrying. It contains the corpus's clearest principled argument against the standard removal test, saying that studying the single individual unaided, stripped of her tools and her social support, means learning is stripped of its essence and is not learning in a genuine sense any more. It gives a mechanism for why a support that guarantees success cannot teach: error variance is the variation, so error is not a by-product of practice but a necessary constitutive element of learning to discern, and a child who hit the target by luck on every throw would learn nothing. And it states a design rule keyed to the designer's ignorance rather than the learner's state, that the less you know what problems people will meet, the more varied the problems you must let them handle. Across sixteen pages the words scaffold, fading, withdraw, gradual and Vygotsky appear zero times; contingent appears once and means conditional on. Its own headline evidence, the variability-of-practice ball-throwing study, is a removal test of exactly the kind the paper argues against.

medium · This is an invited keynote, not a study. The authors run nothing: every empirical claim is a reinterpretation of somebody else's work, reported in a sentence or two with no numbers, no sample sizes and no tests anywhere in the paper. The motor-learning comparison that carries the central argument is attributed to a personal communication and to the variability of practice literature in general, without a citation to a specific experiment; Ueno's frame of reference study is summarised as students having considerably improved, with no measure. Runesson's and McKenzie's studies are described qualitatively from unpublished theses and conference papers. What the paper does have is a stated, falsifiable mechanism and a rule that follows from it, argued consistently across four different domains, and a position on the measurement of learning that no other paper in this corpus states as directly. Take the argument and the position; do not take any of the empirical illustrations as evidence.

sections.title: 5 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.small: concept or lineage, contradiction, open question
items.lead: This is the sharpest statement in the corpus of the position that the review's own measurement rule contradicts. The rule this review has been applying says a learning measure has to be taken after the support ends and outside the arrangement that delivered it. Marton and Trigwell say that arrangement is where the competence is: you cannot drive without a car, and being able to drive is a way of relating to a car. Taken seriously it means the corpus's transfer nulls are partly an artefact of the test, and the withdrawal question has to be restated as which part of a distributed competence a person should end up holding rather than whether they can perform alone. What it does not license is abandoning the removal test, because the paper's own headline evidence is one: the ball-throwing children were scored from a direction neither group had practised. The argument and its exemplar disagree, and the exemplar is the part with data.

rows.value: Against the background of this line of reasoning, taking the single individual unaided doing a task on her own - as is usually done in the study of learning - lacks ecological validity. By stripping the individual of her tools, of her social support and of the meaningfulness of the task, learning is stripped of its essence, it is not learning (in a genuine sense) any more.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: A mechanism, not a preference. Most arguments in this corpus for keeping difficulty in a task come from cognitive load theory or from desirable difficulties, and they say effort is what produces learning. This one says something narrower and more checkable: if what you are learning is to tell one case from another, the spread of your own failures is the variation you learn from, so a support that guarantees a correct outcome has removed the raw material. The thought experiment makes it concrete, a child who hit the target by luck every time learning nothing about the relation between distance and effort. This predicts the pattern the corpus keeps finding, where the arm with the cleanest artefacts does worst on a later unaided task, and it predicts where that pattern will not hold: for supports that carry housekeeping rather than the discrimination the person is meant to own, there is no error variance being suppressed that matters.

rows.value: As the variation in relation to the performance criterion is error variance, we can clearly argue that there is no error-free learning when it comes to learning to discern. It is not just that practise is necessary, and learners make mistakes occasionally, but the fact is that practise without mistakes does not yield learning. Error is thus not a by-product of practise but a necessary constitutive element of learning to discern.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: A design rule for preparation that is keyed to the designer's ignorance rather than to the learner's state, and it is worth carrying precisely because of what it is not. Every contingency rule in this corpus asks what the learner can currently do; this one asks how much the designer knows about the future task, and sets the spread of practice accordingly. That makes it schedulable in advance and checkable without any diagnosis of the learner, which is the bottleneck that has stopped everyone else from building contingent fading. The cost is that nothing in the rule changes as the person improves. The paper's whole apparatus for producing people who can act in unknown future practices contains no step in which support is reduced, and no vocabulary for one: across sixteen pages fading, withdraw, gradual and temporary are all zero. Preparation here is done by widening the variation, not by taking anything away.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: A design-space axis this review can use: what a support supplies. Most of the corpus describes supports that supply part of the product, a hint, a template, a draft, a correction, and every one of them owes a story about what happens when it stops. The supports described here supply contrast instead. A screen that shows the same falling object from three moving frames of reference, or a graph that moves as a child walks, does not do any of the learner's work; it makes an aspect vary that the world holds constant, so the learner can notice it. The consequence for withdrawal is direct. What such a tool leaves behind is a discernment held by the person, so once the aspect has been discerned there is nothing left in the tool that the person still depends on, and removing it is not a test but a formality. That gives a principled reason why some permanent supports are not failures, and it is a different reason from the housekeeping exemption: the tool is not permanent, it is finished.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This gives the review an alternative explanation for its own transfer nulls. The standard reading of a null, when someone trained with support does no better than a control on a new task, is that nothing was internalised. Marton and Trigwell offer another: whether two situations look alike is not a property of the pair but of everything else the person has met, so a person trained on a narrow set will not see the new task as related to anything they know, however well they learned it. That is not a defence of the supports in this corpus, because most of them are delivered on uniform task sets, which is exactly the condition the argument says produces a null. It is a warning about attribution: a transfer failure after narrow training does not distinguish a support that failed to hand over from a training set too uniform to make the handover visible. Any study claiming to test internalisation should say how much its practice varied.

cards.title: Two-Tiered Scaffolding: Congruent Processes of Teaching and Learning. Technical Report No. 523.

rows.value: other
concept or theory, lineage or history, design principle, framework or design space

A 1991 technical report that adds a second storey to the scaffolding metaphor: the first tier is an adult supporting a child, the second is the support an adult needs in order to support a child that way, which in practice means teacher education. Reading Recovery, a one-to-one first-grade reading intervention that typically runs 12 to 16 weeks at 30 minutes a day, is used as the worked example at both tiers. Three things are worth carrying. It states the withdrawal requirement in unusually strong form, that scaffolding must be adjusted over time so responsibility shifts from teacher to child and that the responsibility for adjusting the scaffold itself becomes the learner's, and it then shows the shift running through four concrete stages in a single behaviour, finger-pointing while reading, ending with the child in complete control and free to point again when the text is hard. It gives a criterion for when to move on, unprompted awareness of one's own errors, and a program-level exit rule, children are discontinued when they read at the average level of their classmates. And it names a failure mode still worth quoting: front-loaded, decontextualised strategy instruction confuses means with ends, so a child who can recite a five-step procedure may or may not be able to use it. The paper collects no data of its own; every outcome number in it is a citation to somebody else's study.

high · A conceptual report, classified by ERIC as Reports - Evaluative/Feasibility, that collects nothing. In sixteen pages there is no sample, no design, no condition, no statistic and no test; the two reading transcripts and two teacher-training transcripts are illustrations the authors chose to show the model working, with no account of how they were picked from the thousands of lessons the paper says exist. Every outcome number is borrowed: the 12 to 16 week figure from Pinnell, DeFord and Lyons 1988, and the sole after-support evidence, effects sustained two years past discontinuation, is a one-sentence report of Slavin and Madden 1989 with no effect size, comparison group or page reference. The authors also say Reading Recovery was not built on Vygotsky's theory and that its features may be interpreted in Vygotskian terms, so the worked example is a reinterpretation rather than a test. The weight this bears is definitional and prescriptive: a clear statement of what the construct required in 1991 and a source of design rules specific enough to build. Cite nothing from it as a demonstrated effect.

sections.title: 7 page-grounded claims
sections.note: Each claim keeps the authors' words and the reviewer's interpretation apart, and every excerpt names its page.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: The construct as it stood in 1991, before software design got hold of it, and worth carrying because three constraints are packed into two sentences that later framework papers drop. Support is defined against a counterfactual, the task must be one the learner could not otherwise complete, which excludes convenience. Support is temporary and adjustable rather than a fixed feature of an environment. And the quantity rule is a minimum, not a maximum: give the least that keeps the learner at the upper limit of competence, because anything more is work taken away from them. That is the same instinct as the anti-automation clause in the 2002 Symphony guidelines, and like it, it comes with no way of telling how much is least. Here the gap is admitted rather than hidden, since the paper attributes the judgment to craftsmanship, that is, to a skilled person reading one learner in real time. A reviewer should note what that costs: a definition whose central quantity is set by human judgment cannot be checked, and cannot be transferred to a tool without someone inventing the missing criterion.

From the Vygotskian perspective, a high-craft teacher provides the minimal support necessary to assist a learner to operate at the upper limits of competence. Adjustable scaffolds are temporarily used to help extend the range of work and accomplish tasks not otherwise possible.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.small: concept or lineage, principle, open question
items.lead: The withdrawal requirement, stated as a requirement, and stated one step further than usual. The ordinary version is that responsibility for the task passes to the learner. This paper adds that the responsibility for adjusting the support passes too, so the endpoint of scaffolding is not a learner who no longer needs help but a learner who decides for themselves how much help they need. That is a harder target and a more useful one, because it survives the discovery that supports are rarely removed in practice: a support that stays available but is now governed by the learner has still completed the transfer. Two things bound it. Nothing in the paper detects when the transfer has happened at the level of the whole scaffold, as against the single behaviour worked through elsewhere in the paper, and no evidence is offered that it happens at all. And the vocabulary is worth recording precisely, because it explains why searches of this literature miss papers like this one: in 33,078 folded characters the words fading, fade, withdraw, withdrawal, contingent and contingency do not occur once, while scaffold occurs 47 times and zone of proximal development 12 times. The requirement is here in full; the vocabulary the later literature uses for it is not.

rows.value: Scaffolding must be adjusted over time so that there is a shift in responsibility from the teacher to the child. The child must come to accept the responsibility for all aspects of reading. Whereas the teacher initially adjusted the scaffold relative to the learner's skill as it interacted with task difficulty, the responsibility for flexible adjustment becomes the learner's responsibility.

items.heading: Claim 3 · CLAIM-003
items.lead: The most transferable half-page in the paper, because it is fading actually operationalised rather than merely required. One observable behaviour, four stages, each one nameable: the support is imposed by the helper; then it is made optional and going without it is praised; then the helper stops judging and starts asking the learner to judge, which is the step almost nobody builds; then the learner owns the decision. The endpoint is the second thing worth carrying. It is not zero support. The child reads without pointing most of the time and points again when the text is hard or he is about to lose his place, so what has been withdrawn is the requirement and the prompting, while the capability remains available on demand. That reframes what a review should look for when it asks whether support was faded. Absence is the wrong test; the right one is who decides, and whether the learner reinstates support appropriately. items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: A contingency rule with an observable trigger, which is the thing the design literature almost never supplies. The signal that a support has done its job is not a score, a duration or a designer's schedule but the disappearance of the prompt: when the learner notices their own error without being asked, that support is finished and the helper moves to the next thing. Paired with it is an ownership test that is equally cheap and equally strict, that a correction only counts if the learner initiated it, which rules out the common measurement error of crediting a support with performance it produced by prompting. Both rules are instrumentable outside reading: run the support, then withhold it, and see whether the behaviour survives the withholding. The paper also carries the whole procedure up to its second tier, where trainees are deliberately confronted with mismatches between what they see and what they do, so the same mechanism governs the support and the support's support. What is missing is any calibration. Consistently is not defined, no count of unprompted notices is proposed, and nothing addresses the obvious confound that a learner may stop showing errors because the text got easier.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: This is the paper's only statement about what learners can do once the support is gone, and it is worth recording precisely because of its form. It is a citation, not a finding: one sentence reporting somebody else's synthesis, with no effect size, no comparison, no page reference and no discussion. So this paper does not measure the thing it requires. What it does have, and what most supports in this corpus lack, is the apparatus that makes the question askable at all. The intervention has a defined end and an operational exit criterion, children are discontinued when they read at the average level of their first-grade peers, and the program's stated aim is a self-improving system rather than a performance while supported. Once support has a termination point and a criterion for reaching it, a follow-up study is possible; where support is an always-present feature of a tool, as in most of the software literature, there is no after in which to measure anything. That is the transferable point: designing an exit is a precondition for ever knowing whether the support worked, and it is a design decision rather than an evaluation one.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: A failure mode named in 1991 that the rest of this corpus keeps rediscovering. A support that hands over an explicit procedure can leave the learner able to recite it and unable to run it, because reciting the recipe has quietly become the task. Two things make this more than a slogan. First, it identifies the mechanism as task substitution rather than insufficient help: the support did not fail to teach, it taught something else, and the learner's fluent performance of the wrong thing is what conceals the failure. Second, the predicted cost is specifically to maintenance and generalization, that is, to exactly the horizons that go unmeasured when evaluation stops at the end of the supported session. So the failure is not merely undetected by such evaluations, it is invisible to them by construction, since during support the recipe-reciting learner performs well. The claim is asserted, attributed to Duffy and to Stone, and tested nowhere in this paper, which is a real limit on citing it; but as a hypothesis it is precise enough to test and predicts a specific dissociation between recall of a procedure and use of it.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The paper's own contribution, and the reason it is worth a card rather than a context note. The move is to say that a support needs supporting: if the first-tier method is judgment-heavy, then whatever produces the judgment is part of the design, and it is built as a connected upper storey rather than a separate structure. The authors are explicit that the same withdrawal requirement runs at both levels, so the trainer's support of the teacher is as temporary as the teacher's support of the child. For a review of supports for human work that matters in two ways. It gives a vocabulary for the layer almost every study omits, the preparation and ongoing coaching that a support's effectiveness silently depends on, and it explains why results from human-delivered supports transfer so badly to tools: the tool has no second tier, and the paper's own account of the first tier says the method is teacher-dependent, not teacher-proof, and cannot be delivered as a kit or a fixed sequence. The framing is motivated by a warning worth keeping in its own right, Wertsch's, that leaving the adult's role poorly defined risks making the zone of proximal development too broad to be useful. That is the earliest statement in this corpus of the problem this review exists to address, and this paper's answer only half addresses it: it specifies who supports the supporter without narrowing what counts as support.

cards.title: Scaffolding: Observing and Responding to Young Children Learning to Read by Reading.

rows.value: S2W-DD8FADC6B8DFCD59AA864724
other
concept or theory, lineage or history, primary empirical

A conference paper from November 1984 that catches the word scaffolding in the act of changing domains. Bruner and colleagues had coined it for how adults support a young child's spoken communicative intentions; Pappas argues it should frame early literacy too, and reports kindergarten children re-reading picture books they had been read aloud. Across successive re-readings the children's versions move closer to the structure the author actually used. Two things make it worth carrying. It preserves Bruner's 1983 two-thread structure, an external thread about how the community arranges encounters and an internal one about how communicative intent is transformed through negotiation into increasingly powerful procedures, which is a developmental account located in the learner rather than in the support. And even here, a year before the term became ubiquitous and written by someone reading Bruner directly, there is no vocabulary of withdrawal: handover, fading, gradual, responsibility, independence and contingency each occur zero times in twenty-seven pages. The paper closes by attacking the basal readers of the day as not being stories at all, which makes the support conditional on there being real structure to work on.

high · Read as evidence about children this is very weak and does not pretend otherwise. It is an unrefereed conference talk with no method section, no stated sample beyond six named children, no coding procedure, no comparison and no measure; the findings are illustrative transcripts of individual children's successive re-readings with the author pointing at what changed. Read as evidence about the concept it is strong and hard to get elsewhere: a dated, primary application of Bruner's formulation by someone working directly from his 1983 text, at the moment the term crossed from oral language into literacy. Everything on this card is a lineage or definitional claim for that reason, and the one empirical observation is recorded with its limits attached. The OCR layer also carries errors, so quoted passages contain scanning artifacts.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: A dated instance of the term crossing domains, with the crossing argued rather than assumed. Scaffolding was coined to describe adults supporting a child's spoken communicative intentions; this paper transposes it to reading and writing on the explicit grounds that an analogous external thread must occur for literacy. That is an argument from structural similarity, not from evidence that the same mechanism operates, and it is the kind of move every later extension of the term rests on: from literacy to software, from software to tutoring systems, from there to AI assistants. Worth recording because the review needs to know where the elasticity entered, and the answer is that it was there almost immediately, one year after Bruner's 1983 restatement and by an author working directly from it.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: Bruner's formulation, preserved here, has two halves that later definitions do not. The external half is the arrangement of encounters, which is roughly what everyone since has meant by scaffolding: the supporter sets things up so the task becomes possible. The internal half is the one that vanishes, and it is not a withdrawal account. It locates the change over time in the learner, whose communicative intent is transformed through negotiation into increasingly powerful procedures, rather than in the supporter doing progressively less. That reframes what the corpus has been finding. The problem is not that a fading criterion was dropped from a fuller original; it is that the original's dynamic lived in the learner's growing capability, later definitions kept only the arrangement half, and nothing replaced the developmental half at all. A framework with an external thread and no internal one has no account of why the support should ever change.

rows.value: The first thread, the external thread, describes how the linguistic community arranges speech encounters so that the young aspirant speaker can get a hold on how to make his own communicative intentions clear and how to penetrate the intentions of others. This second thread, according to Bruner (1983), is an internal or procedural one... concerned with how communicative intent is successively transformed through negotiation into increasingly powerful linguistic procedures.

items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: Read as a design claim rather than a polemic, this is a scope condition. If the mechanism is that a child progressively approximates the structure an author used, then it requires an author who used a structure, and the basal passages the paper reproduces have none: the reproduced texts are word lists arranged into sentences about liking fish and stopping vehicles. The support therefore does not act on the learner alone; it acts on the learner and the material together, and degrading the material defeats it however well the adult behaves. That generalises usefully. Any support whose mechanism is convergence on a model is only as good as the model, and evaluations that hold the support constant while simplifying the material to make the study tractable are removing the thing the mechanism runs on. The complaint about teachers having no time is separate and is asserted, not evidenced.

cards.title: Structure-mapping: A theoretical framework for analogy

rows.value: other
concept or theory, framework or design space, measurement or method, primary empirical

The 1983 paper that gave analogy a mechanism. Knowledge is represented as propositional networks of nodes and predicates, with two syntactic distinctions doing all the work: attributes take one argument and relations take two or more, and higher-order predicates take propositions rather than objects. Three mapping rules follow. Discard the attributes of objects. Try to preserve the relations between them. And to choose among relations, take systems of them, because a predicate belonging to a mappable system of mutually interconnecting relationships is more likely to be imported than an isolated one. The discriminating case is one comparison: between sun and planet both MORE MASSIVE THAN and HOTTER THAN hold, and only the first transfers to the atom, because only the first participates in the central-force system. Figure 1 draws the loss, the target network being the source with the attribute cluster and one relation deleted. The rules read only the syntax of the representation and never its content, which the author defends by rejecting the two content-sensitive alternatives as mistakes. A four-cell taxonomy falls out, literal similarity, analogy, mere appearance match and anomaly, with analogy and literal similarity a continuum rather than a dichotomy. And a conjecture closes it: learners move from literal similarity through analogy to general laws, because too much overlap hides what is crucial while a sparse shared structure can be analysed.

low · The theory is stated with unusual precision: three rules, one selection principle, two syntactic distinctions, a four-cell taxonomy and a figure that draws the mapping. The discriminating case, mass transferring where temperature does not, is decisive against the alternative on offer. Two things are thin and the card marks them: the empirical support is one unquantified correlation, and the analogical shift conjecture is labelled informal and rests on a single observed subject. Note also that page 1 of this scan has a corrupted text layer, so every quotation on this card is drawn from the clean body pages rather than the abstract.

items.heading: Claim 1 · CLAIM-001
items.lead: Three rules that turn analogy from an intuition into an operation. What crosses between domains is the relations among objects, not the properties of the objects, and Figure 1 draws the consequence: the atom network is the solar-system network with the attribute cluster and one relation deleted. That batteries and reservoirs are both cylindrical would not support their analogy and differing shapes would not weaken it; in 3:6::2:4 only the relation twice as great as counts, and 3:6::200:400 is no worse even though 3 shares more features with 2 than with 200. Any account that counts shared features has to get those cases wrong.

items.heading: Claim 2 · CLAIM-002
items.lead: The whole theory in one comparison, and it is falsifiable. Between sun and planet both MORE MASSIVE THAN and HOTTER THAN hold, both are relations rather than attributes, and both could in principle map to the atom. Only the first does, because only the first belongs to the interconnected system in which changing one relation changes the others: weaken the attraction and the distance grows, reverse which body is more massive and you reverse which revolves around which. No account based on counting shared predicates can produce that difference. The second worked case generalises it: of two scenarios about water, the punctured vessel transfers and the lidded one does not, because causal structure sits more deeply embedded than static spatial structure.

rows.value: I propose the systematicity principle: A predicate that belongs to a mappable system of mutually interconnecting relationships is more likely to be imported into the target than is an isolated predicate. This is why MORE MASSIVE THAN is preserved while HOTTER THAN is not: Only MORE MASSIVE THAN participates in the central-force system of predicates.

items.lead: This is what makes structure-mapping an engineering proposition rather than a description of a human habit. items.heading: Claim 4 · CLAIM-004
items.lead: A four-cell taxonomy of comparison on two axes a designer can manipulate: how much attribute overlap a representation exposes, and how much relational overlap. Many of both is literal similarity, many relations and few attributes is analogy, many attributes and few relations is a mere appearance match whose explanatory power the author calls sharply limited, and neither is anomaly. Abstraction is a fifth reading distinguished by the base having few attributes too. The load-bearing line is that relational overlap is necessary for any strong sense of similarity at all, which says a support surfacing only surface features will produce comparisons that feel apt and explain nothing. And analogy and literal similarity are a continuum rather than a dichotomy, so a coding scheme built on this has to record two quantities rather than choose a label.

rows.value: Overlap in relations is necessary for any strong perception of similarity between two domains. Overlap in both object-attributes and inter-object relationships is seen as literal similarity, and overlap in relationships but not objects is seen as analogical relatedness. Overlap in object-attributes but not relationships is seen as a mere appearance match. Finally, a comparison with neither attribute overlap nor relational overlap is simply an anomaly.

items.heading: Claim 5 · CLAIM-005
items.lead: The most consequential idea here for a review of how support should change over a learner's trajectory, and the author labels it an informal observation from one subject. The sequence is literal similarity, then analogy, then general law, and each step has a stated reason. Literal similarity is easy to find and useless for isolating principles, because there is too much overlap to know what is crucial. Analogy is hard to find, since it requires reaching the knowledge base through relational matches where object matches are of no use, and is far more useful once found, because the shared structure is sparse enough to analyse. A general law is not a better analogy but a different construction: the person must build a new relational structure whose objects are stripped of specific attributes. So the same externalised representation is worth different amounts at different stages, and the hard transitions are noticing a relational match and stripping a structure of its objects.

rows.value: An informal observation is that the earliest comparisons are chiefly literal-similarity matches, followed by analogies, followed by general laws. However, once found, an analogy should be more useful in deriving the key principles, since the shared data structure is sparse enough to permit analysis. To state a general law requires another step beyond creating a temporary correspondence betweeen unlike domains: The person must create a new relational structure whose objects are so lacking in specific attributes that the structure can be applied across widely different domains.

items.heading: Claim 6 · CLAIM-006
items.lead: The commitment that keeps this a psychological theory rather than a formalism about propositions, and it is also the theory's softest joint. Everything rests on the attribute-relation distinction, and the paper's own footnote concedes that logically a relation can be re-encoded as a one-place predicate that is true exactly when the relation holds. So nothing in logic fixes the distinction; only how a person happens to construe the domain does. The paper handles the awkward cases by the same standard: LARGE means large for its class and so implicitly compares, but is processed as an attribute because the comparison reaches outside the domain of discourse, while LARGER THAN between two objects inside it is processed as a relation. That is a coherent rule and it makes the representation an empirical claim about a particular person's construal, which nothing here measures.

items.heading: Claim 7 · CLAIM-007
items.lead: The paper's empirical footing and its account of why the competition could not have found the same thing. The reported result is one correlation, that people rate as most apt the analogies about which they write the most relational information, given in a paragraph without statistics. It is consistent with the theory and does not distinguish it from any account in which relational content drives aptness. What the survey of neighbouring work adds is a representational diagnosis: feature lists and multidimensional spaces handle object attributes well and are extremely limited at expressing relations between objects, especially higher-order ones, so a field working with those representations could not have formulated systematicity at all. The author is candid that most of the theoretically richer work in the area remains interesting but unvalidated.

rows.value: Further, a correlation of aptness ratings and relationality ratings revealed that subjects rated as most apt those analogies for which they wrote the greatest amount of relational information. These kinds of representations can deal well with object attributes, but are extremely limited in their ability to express relations between objects, and especially higher-order relations.
